Takeaway


Computational reproducibility specifically requires obtaining the same results using the same data and same code/analysis.





Point out that terms like “reproducible” and “replicable” are often used interchangeably in lay conversations, but The Turing Way establishes precise definitions along a 2x2 grid.
Walk through each quadrant:

Reproducible: Same data + Same code. This is our baseline standard in computational data science.
Replicable: Different data + Same pipeline. Tests if the finding holds up in a new sample or dataset.
Robust: Same data + Different pipeline. Tests if the finding is an artifact of a specific software package, model choice, or script.
Generalisable: Different data + Different pipeline. The gold standard for scientific claims.

Remind students: In this course, we focus heavily on the top-left quadrant (Reproducibility) as the foundation for all the others.

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
Reproducible \(\neq\) Open Data

Open Science promotes making data, code, and papers freely available to everyone.
Computational Reproducibility focuses on code execution logic, pipeline integrity, and environment preservation.
A project with restricted or sensitive data (e.g., medical, commercial) can still be fully reproducible through:

Synthetic test datasets.
Containerized environments (Docker).
Secure, audited execution pipelines.




Address a common student misconception: “My dataset has human subjects / proprietary business data, so I can’t make my project reproducible.”
Clarify that Open and Reproducible overlap, but are distinct concepts.
Explain how to make restricted data projects reproducible:

Provide synthetic or scrambled mock data that mirrors the schema so external users can verify the code runs.
Write deterministic unit tests and containerize the environment.
Ensure that an authorized auditor inside a secure enclave could re-run the exact script and get identical results.

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
Reproducibility as “Personal Insurance”
Working reproducibly benefits you (and your team) first:

Future-proofing: Your primary collaborator six months from now is your future self.
Seamless onboarding: New lab members can run existing pipelines without months of reconstruction.
Error resilience: Automated pipelines make updating figures or fixing small bugs fast and low-risk.



Frame reproducibility not as an altruistic duty for science, but as self-preservation.
Ask the class: “Have you ever opened a project you worked on 6 months ago and spent 2 hours trying to remember which script to run first?”
Emphasize “Your future self doesn’t reply to emails.” If you don’t document relative paths, dependencies, and execution order today, your future self will suffer.
Mention that automated pipelines (like Make or targets in R) allow you to re-render an entire 50-page manuscript or dashboard with one command after updating raw data.

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
The “Added Advantage”: Credit & Citation
Publishing reproducible workflows directly boosts academic impact:

Higher Citations: Papers with public code and data receive demonstrably higher citation rates.
Greater Trust: Independent researchers can audit, verify, and build directly on your work.
Secondary Outputs: Reusable R packages, Python libraries, and pipelines earn recognition as first-class scientific contributions.



Highlight the selfish incentives for doing open/reproducible work: literature consistently shows a “citation advantage” for papers with publicly available code and data repositories.
Explain that code repositories (GitHub/Zenodo with DOIs) allow other researchers to cite your tools even if they aren’t citing your specific empirical findings.
Trust is currency in science: when readers can inspect your raw scripts and computational pipeline, they treat your findings with far higher confidence.

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
Barrier: The “Career Tax” & Incentive Gap

Publication Bias: Academic hiring, tenure, and grants overwhelmingly reward novel findings over robust software engineering or replication studies.
The Time Sink: Documenting code, setting up continuous integration, and containerizing environments takes significant time.
Incentive Gap: Without institutional rewards, researchers view reproducible practices as an unrewarded “career tax.”



Connect this to real-world career incentives (hiring, tenure, grant funding).
Point out the tension: Building a clean, modular, fully tested pipeline takes 2-3x longer than writing a quick “one-off” messy script.
If hiring committees only count the number of novel publications on a resume, the researcher who takes shortcuts will publish faster than the researcher who builds reproducible infrastructure.
Ask the class: “How do we fix this incentive structure in data science and computational fields?”

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
Barrier: Resource & Infrastructure Deficits
Reproducibility requires resources that are often underfunded or unevenly distributed:

Skills Gap: Training in software engineering (Git, virtual environments, pipelines) is rarely built into scientific curricula.
Computing Costs: Heavy computational pipelines (e.g., multi-GPU training) can be financially prohibitive to re-run or audit.
Maintenance: Software dependencies drift over time, requiring continuous maintenance to stay executable.



Summarize the physical and structural resource barriers:

Knowledge gap: Most domain scientists were never formally taught Git, Docker, or environment isolation—they are self-taught out of necessity.
Financial/Compute gap: Re-running a deep learning model or climate simulation might cost thousands of dollars in cloud computing credits.
Dependency drift: R packages and Python libraries update constantly. A script written in 2020 may fail in 2026 if packages aren’t pinned (renv/uv/conda).

Conclude by setting up the transition to the next part of your course: teaching the practical tools (Git, Quarto, environments) that help overcome these exact barriers.

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
Screens Off, Minds On



Devices Away: Laptops & tablets closed, phones away.
No One Alone: Pair or team up (no solo seats).
Engage Fully: Be ready to speak, debate, and share ideas.

Scenario A
Two candidates are competing for a single tenure-track position:


Candidate A publishes 5 papers a year. Their code is undocumented, scattered across local desktop folders, and missing computational environments, but their results are novel and published in high-impact venues.



Candidate B publishes 2 papers a year. Every project features fully documented Quarto/Jupyter workflows, continuous integration tests, archived Docker containers on Zenodo, and granular version control.




The hiring committee selects Candidate A, citing their superior “publication volume and research productivity.”

title: Guide for Reproducible Research
text:
Scenario C
A research group in climate modeling trains a deep learning architecture for 6 days across a cluster of 32 GPUs, costing $15,000 in cloud compute credits.
A peer reviewer asks the team to re-run the entire pipeline with three alternative random seed initializations to prove statistical stability.
The group’s grant budget is exhausted, and their compute allocation has expired.


Describe at least 2 things that the research group can provide to peer reviewers to prove their pipeline is trustworthy.



Intermediate State Archiving: Saving and publishing model checkpoints, raw log outputs, and loss curves on repositories like Zenodo/OSF.
Dry-Run / Toy Pipelines: Providing a fast, low-compute “mock” version of the pipeline using a small synthetic dataset so others can verify the code logic end-to-end in seconds.
Deterministic Sub-sampling: Demonstrating stability on a lightweight, representative subset of the data before scaling up to full GPU clusters.
Environment & Seed Logging: Strictly archiving the exact container image (Docker), fixed random seeds, and hardware specs so that even if others can’t run it now, the execution state is perfectly preserved for the future.

title: Review
text:
The Bulk “Submit Button” Commit

No Rollback Capability: If an analysis script breaks at hour 10, a bulk commit forces you to discard everything rather than rewinding to a functional state.
Opaque Collaboration: In group settings, bulk commits create massive merge conflicts and hide individual provenance.
Data Dumping: Bulk commits often accidentally check in binary outputs, credentials, or multi-gigabyte raw files.

title: Review
text:
Atomic Commits
An atomic commit encapsulates one logical unit of work e.g.,

"adding a data preprocessing function"
"fixing a plotting script bug"
"updating the environment.yml"

title: Review
text:
Advantages of Atomic Commits
If you commit:

a bug fix,
an environment change,
and a data-cleaning script

in three separate commits, you can easily revert just the broken data-cleaning script (git revert <commit-hash>) while keeping your bug fix intact.

title: Review
text:
Bulk Commits (Don’t ❗️)


While taking a “snapshot” of several (e.g. 10) modified files at the end of a long work session feels convenient, it breaks the core benefits of version control.

Why?
If all 10 changes live in a single massive commit, reverting the bug means throwing away hours of unrelated, functional work—or manually sifting through hundreds of lines of code to fix it by hand.

title: Review
text:
Bulk Commits (Don’t ❗️)


With bulk commits a reviewer cannot meaningfully audit a single pull request or commit that reads:
+12,450 lines / -3,200 lines across 40 files.



Smaller, logical commits tell a readable story. A reviewer can follow your thought process step-by-step rather than drowning in a massive wall of code differences (git diff)

title: Review
text:
Bulk Commits (Don’t ❗️)
When working on collaborative projects or multi-branch workflows:
Smaller, frequent commits touch fewer lines of code at a time, making automatic merges smooth.
When you finally push a bulk commit, it frequently conflicts with your collaborators’ work, creating complex merge conflicts that require hours of manual reconstruction.

title: Review
section: Risk of Accidental File Leaks & Repository Bloat
text:
Risk of Accidental File Leaks & Repository Bloat
When developers run git add . and commit everything in bulk without inspecting their staging area, they frequently check in files that should never enter version control:

Large Datasets / Binaries: Large CSVs, SQLite databases, or model weights that permanently bloat the .git folder history.
System junk: .DS_Store files, build artifacts, or temporary editor files.
Sensitive Information: API keys, passwords, or local file system path configurations.

title: Review
text:
Rule of Thumb


As a rule of thumb, one commit should represent one logical unit of work.


A Good Test: If your commit message needs the word “AND” to describe what you did (e.g., "Cleaned data matrix AND added plotting script AND updated environment specs"), it should be split into three separate commits.

title: Review
text:
The “README as an API” Principle


A README.md is not just a summary cover sheet; it is the instruction manual for your computational pipeline.

title: Review
text:
5+1 mandatory sections in README

Title
Overview (about)
Repository structure (file structure)
Environment setup
Reproduction instructions
License*

title: Review
text:
Filestructure in README
Benefits:

Establishes Instant Spatial Orientation (Mental Model)
Clarifies Data Provenance & File Roles
Discovers Relative Paths & Eliminates Path Confusion
Serves as Self-Documenting Infrastructure
Exposes Messy Repository Hygiene (The “Messy Room” Test)

title: Review
text:
Establishes Instant Spatial Orientation (Mental Model)
When a collaborator, reviewer, or grader clones your repository, they are looking at a blank slate.

Without a tree, they have to manually click through nested subfolders to figure out where scripts, datasets, and configurations reside.
A directory tree provides a 3-second visual map of the entire codebase. It immediately communicates the project’s layout without requiring the reader to explore the file system manually.

title: Review
text:
Clarifies Data Provenance & File Roles
Filename extensions (like .csv, .py, .ipynb, or .rds) don’t tell the full story of why a file exists or how it should be treated.

Separating Raw vs. Processed Data: A directory tree visually enforces the golden rule of reproducible research: raw data must be immutable. Annotating data/raw/ in your tree explicitly warns users never to overwrite original files.
Distinguishing Source Code from Notebooks: It clarifies which files are modular, reusable scripts (e.g., scripts/clean_data.py) versus interactive exploratory narratives (e.g., notebooks/exploratory.ipynb).

title: Review
text:
Closing Thoughts

Writing clean code is only half the battle in modern data science.




If your work cannot be re-built automatically by an independent researcher using your version-control record and environment specs, the results are incomplete.




Treat your repository as a publication in itself.

It controls how your package interacts with the rest of the R ecosystem

#' @title Average
#' @description Computes the average (i.e. mean)
#' @param x input vector
#' @param na.rm whether to remove missing values
#' @return computed mean
#' @export
average <- function(x, na.rm = FALSE) {
  # decide whether to remove missing values
  if (na.rm) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  }
  # compute average
  avg <- sum(x) / length(x)
  return(avg)
}

Minimal file structure
You can create the minimal file structure of an R package by hand, e.g.


Terminal

mkdir average
cd average
touch DESCRIPTION NAMESPACE
mkdir R man


However, we recommend that you use functions from packages "devtools" and "usethis" to create and take care of the files and directories in an R package.

title: R Packaging
text:
About
I will describe one way to create some of the common elements of an R package, and also a development workflow to iterate through the packaging process.
Keep in mind that there are various ways to create an R package, and that you are not required to use "devtools" and friends.
But as you’ll see, these supporting packages are extremely helpful, and will take care of many of the important details, and “pain points” of packaging your code.

Step 1) create_package()

Instead of creating the file structure of an R package by hand, we’ll use create_package()
You have to invoke this function on R’s console, by passing the file path (location and name) of the package you want to create


# use a valid file path to your package
usethis::create_package("path/to/average")

BTW: You only run this function once!

Step 3.1) Creating Unit Tests

As you define functions in your package—in the files below R/—you add the corresponding tests to .R files in tests/testthat/.
It is recommended that the organization of test files match the organization of R/ files.
For example, since we have R/average.R, there should be a corresponding test file in tests/testthat/test-average.R
The easiest way to setup the test file is by running usethis::use_test("average")

Running tests

Depending on where you are in the development cycle, you’ll run your tests at various scales.
When you are rapidly iterating on a function, you might work at the level of individual tests.
As the code settles down, you’ll run entire test files and eventually the entire test suite.
Micro-iteration: This is the interactive phase where you initiate and refine a function and its tests in tandem.

Run devtools::load_all() often
Then execute individual expectations or whole tests interactively in the console

Data

Sometimes you may want to include data in a package.
Examples:

mpg data in package "ggplot2"

BTW: some packages exist solely for the purpose of distributing data

e.g. "babynames", "stat20data"

More info about data at: https://r-pkgs.org/data.html

Storing R objects in data/

The most common location for package data is data/.
We recommend that each file in this directory be an .rda file created by save() containing a single R object, with the same name as the file.
The easiest way to achieve this is with usethis::use_data().


set.seed(159)
sample_vector <- sample(100)
usethis::use_data(sample_vector)




sample_table <- data.frame(
  x = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 20), 
  y = 20:1)
usethis::use_data(sample_table)

Documenting datasets: roxygen comments
There are two roxygen tags that are especially important for documenting datasets:

@format gives an overview of the dataset.

For data frames, you should include a definition list that describes each variable.
It’s usually a good idea to describe variables’ units here.

@source provides details of where you got the data, often a URL.
Never @export a data set.

text:
Storing Raw Data
In addition to storing “clean” data in data/, you may want to store the script containing the code that generated the data.
In our example, it would be nice to store the code that generates sample_table and sample_vector

sample_table <- data.frame(
  x = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 20), 
  y = 20:1)
usethis::use_data(sample_table)

set.seed(159)
sample_vector <- sample(100)
usethis::use_data(sample_vector)

This is possible via usethis::use_data_raw()

title: R Packaging
text:
Storing Raw Data

usethis::use_data_raw() creates a directory data-raw/
This directory should be listed in .Rbuildignore
The good news is that usethis::use_data_raw() does this for you.
Running this command will give you an output like this:



usethis::use_data_raw("samples")
✔ Creating data-raw/.
✔ Adding "^data-raw$" to .Rbuildignore.
✔ Writing data-raw/samples.R.
☐ Modify data-raw/samples.R.
☐ Finish writing the data preparation script in data-raw/samples.R.
☐ Use `usethis::use_data()` to add prepared data to package.


This will create a samples.R file inside data-raw/.
Here, we can store the commands that generate the sample objects.

title: R Packaging
section: Storing Raw Data in CSV files
text:
Storing Raw Data in CSV files

Another common situation for storing data is when you have a dataset, (e.g. data in a CSV file), that you want to include in your package.
For instance, say we have some data about basketball players in a CSV file basketball.csv.
We need to store basketball.csv inside data-raw/, and then update the code of the R file samples.R

title: R Packaging
section: Storing Raw Data in CSV files
text:
Storing Raw Data in CSV files
Assuming basketball.csv is stored in data-raw/, we edit samples.R as follows:




samples.R

sample_table <- data.frame(
  x = seq(-5, 5, length.out = 20), 
  y = 20:1)
usethis::use_data(sample_table)

set.seed(159)
sample_vector <- sample(100)
usethis::use_data(sample_vector)

basketball <- read.csv("basketball.csv")
usethis::use_data(basketball)


usethis::use_data(basketball) will create basketball.rda inside data/, and also the corresponding basketball.R inside R/ that needs to be edited (to include its documentation with Roxygen comments).

title: Variables in Make
text:
User Defined Variables

In addition to the automatic variables, it is also possible to create our own variables in a Makefile.
We’ll review 2 ways to define variables:

NAME = VALUE
NAME := VALUE

By convention, variable names are always written in UPPERCASE to distinguish them from file targets and commands. However, you can also write them in lowercase.
Likewise, variables are defined at the beginning of the Makefile.
To use a variable inside a target or a recipe, you must wrap its name in parentheses or braces preceded by a dollar sign: $(NAME) or ${NAME}

title: Variables in Make
text:
Example of recursive assignment =
Consider again the situation in which various md files will be assembled by pandoc into an output report.html



Makefile

# Define user variables at the top of the file
MDS = part1.md part2.md part3.md

# generate report.html
report.html: $(MDS)
  pandoc $^ -o $@


In this case we are using = to define MDS. This is a recursive assignment
The value is evaluated lazily at the exact moment the variable is used in a recipe, not when it is defined.

title: Variables in Make
text:
Example of simple expansion :=
Consider again the situation in which various md files will be assembled by pandoc into an output report.html


Makefile

# Define user variables at the top of the file
MDS := part1.md part2.md part3.md

# generate report.html
report.html: $(MDS)
  pandoc $^ -o $@


In this case we are using := to define MDS. This is a simple expansion
The value is evaluated immediately on the spot. This prevents unexpected side effects in long files.

title: Variables in Make
text:
Issue


Makefile

# Not exactly what we think it means
MDS = *.md

# generate report.html
report.html: $(MDS)
  pandoc $^ -o $@


The rule works because the pandoc command accepts wildcards *. But there’s a catch.
⚠️ The issue with the above variable MDS = *.md is that a Make variable represents a string of text.
This means that MDS has the string value *.md instead of part1.md part2.md part3.md

title: Variables in Make
text:
Solution: Wildcard Function
To create a variable MDS that actually gathers the names of the md files, you need to use a special function in Make called the wildcard function:



Makefile

# correct way to "gather" all md files
MDS = $(wildcard *.md)

# generate report.html
report.html: $(MDS)
  pandoc $^ -o $@

title: Naming Files
text:
Unix file naming

Maximum of 255 characters
Avoid most symbols: \ / * & % ? $ | ^ ~ < >
Use A-Z, a-z, 0-9, period, underscore, hyphen
Don’t use a hyphen - as the first character
Prefer lower case letters: MyFile vs myfile

because of case sensitivity

More important: be consistent and stick to a naming style.
Good idea to use file extensions

e.g. .txt, .csv, .html, .md, .pdf, .jpg

title: Naming Files
text:
Checklist

Spend time planning out both folder hierarchy and file naming conventions in the beginning of a project.
Consider how you or others will look for and access files at a later date.
Do you think about them by type, location, study or something else?
Establish a folder hierarchy that aligns with the project.
Consider all aspects of the project and develop a file naming scheme that includes important metadata.

title: Naming Files
text:
Checklist (cont’d)

Consider sorting when deciding what element of the file name will go first.
File names starting with YYYYMM will sort differently than files starting with the MMDDYYYY format.
Provide a method for easy adoption.
Consider a readme file in onboarding documentation for new contributors.
Check for established file naming conventions. Many disciplines have recommendations

title: Naming Files
text:
1) What information (metadata) is important?

Ideally, pick three pieces of metadata; use no more than five.
This metadata should be enough for you to visually scan the file names and easily understand what’s in each one.
Example: For my images, I want to know date, sample ID, and image number for that sample on that date.

title: Naming Files
section: 2) Do you need to abbreviate any of the metadata or encode it?
text:
2) Do you need to abbreviate any of the metadata or encode it?

If any of the metadata from step 1 is described by lots of text, decide what shortened information to keep.
If any of the metadata from step 1 has regular categories, standardize the categories and/or replace them with 2- or 3-letter codes; be sure to document these codes.
Example: Sample ID will use a code made up of: a 2-letter project abbreviation (project 1 = P1, project 2 = P2); a 3-letter species abbreviation (mouse = “MUS”, fruit fly = “DRS”); and 3-digit sample ID (assigned in my notebook).

title: Naming Files
section: 3) What is the order for the metadata in the file name?
text:
3) What is the order for the metadata in the file name?

Think about how you want to sort and search for your files to decide what metadata should appear at the beginning of the file name.
If date is important, use ISO 8601-formatted dates (YYYYMMDD or YYYY-MM-DD) at the beginning of the file names so dates sort chronologically.
Example 1: My sample ID is most important so I will list it first, followed by date, then image number

title: Naming Files
section: 4) What characters will you use to separate each piece of metadata in the file name?
text:
4) What characters will you use to separate each piece of metadata in the file name?

Many computer systems cannot handle spaces in file names.
To make file names both computer- and human-readable, use dashes (-), underscores (_), and/or capitalize the first letter of each word in the file names.
Example: I will use underscores to separate metadata and dashes between parts of my sample ID.

title: Naming Files
section: 5) Will you need to track different versions of each file?
text:
5) Will you need to track different versions of each file?

You can track versions of a file by appending version information to end of the file name.
Consider using a version number (e.g. v01) or the version date (use ISO 8601 format: YYYYMMDD or YYYY-MM-DD).
Example: As each image goes through my analysis workflow, I will append the version type to the end of the file name (e.g. _raw, _processed, and _composite)

title: Naming Files
section: 6) Write down your naming convention pattern.
text:
6) Write down your naming convention pattern.

Make sure the convention only uses alphanumeric characters, dashes, and underscores. Ideally, file names will be 32 characters or less.
Example: my file naming convention is

SA-MPL-EID_YYYYMMDD_###_status.tif

Examples are P1-MUS023_20200229_051_raw.tif and P2-DRS-285_20191031_062_composite.tif

title: Intro to Git (part 1)
text:
What about git’s DAG model?

There’s one root commit (initial commit)
Arrows always point backward in time (from the child commit to its parent)
Why? Because a parent commit cannot know its future children, but a child commit always knows exactly who its parent was.
There are no loops or cycles (a child node cannot be the parent of its parent, or the ancestor of its ancestors)
Each commit has a HASH id (and other metadata)
There are moving pointers (or labels) such as:

HEAD: “You are here” bookmark
main: name of default branch

title: Irreproducibility Tales (part I)

Overview





In 2010, Harvard economists Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff (R&R) published an influential paper claiming that countries with public debt over 90% of GDP experience negative economic growth.

title: Irreproducibility Tales (part I)
text:
Overview




This study was widely cited by politicians to justify harsh post-recession austerity cuts.

title: Irreproducibility Tales (part I)
text:
Replication Attempt
Years later, graduate student Thomas Herndon tried to replicate the study of Reinhart & Rogoff for a class project and failed.

He found various problems:

Selective exclusion of available data
Coding errors
Inappropriate weighting of summary statistics





His conclusion: Over 1946–2009, countries with public debt/GDP ratios above 90% averaged 2.2% real annual GDP growth, not −0.1% as published

title: Irreproducibility Tales (part I)
text:
One of the issues
Thomas Herndon discovered that R&R had accidentally missed five major countries when dragging down their AVERAGE() formula row.
Correcting this basic clerical error completely reversed their main conclusion.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:

Title: Ten Simple Rules for Reproducible Computational Research
Author(s): Sandve G.K., Nekrutenki A., Taylor J., Hovig E.
Year: 2013
Journal: PLOS Computational Biology 9(10): e1003285
https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003285

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Why are we here?

Beyond Morality: Reproducibility isn’t just a moral obligation to your field; a lack of tracking is a direct technical burden on you.
The Time-Saver: Meticulous tracking allows your future self to effortlessly apply past methods to new data or reuse code templates across separate projects.
The Bare-Minimum Threshold: At an absolute baseline, you must at least be able to reproduce your own results to defend your science against future questioning.
The Reality Check: Because any given analysis contains an exponential combination of parameters and software variables, memory will fail you. You must record details while underway.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Rules 1 & 2: Eliminating Human Drift

The Documentation Trap: Manual logs easily drift out of sync.
The Executable Solution: Write your entire workflow as a directly executable file—such as a shell script or a Makefile.
Ban Manual Clicks: Avoid manual copy-pasting, mouse clicks or graphical format tweaks between documents.


Rules 3 & 4: Freezing Your Software State

The Version Lock: Minor changes between software updates can alter data outputs or prevent code from running entirely.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
section: Rule 5: Exposing the Pipeline’s Inner Mechanics
text:
Rule 5: Exposing the Pipeline’s Inner Mechanics




The Analytical Value
Quickly browsing through step-by-step intermediate output files can reveal silent logical discrepancies, catching bugs that are completely masked in final summary charts.

The Pipeline Value
If your full project execution is long or resource-heavy, archiving standardized intermediate states allows you to re-run localized parts of the process without starting over from scratch.


The Audit Baseline: Storing intermediate files allows external peers to critically examine your complete pipeline logic without needing all your local executables operational.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Rules 6 & 7: Perfect Replications & Data Foundations






Rule 6: The Random Seed Mandate


Many analyses involve stochastic element randomness. To achieve an exact procedural reproduction rather than just an approximation, you must explicitly record and pass your initial random seed.




Isolate Visual Tweaks: Store the data behind your charts.
The Scripted Plot: Preserve the exact code used to render a graphic.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
section: Rule 10: Providing Public Access to Your Workflow
text:
Rule 10: Providing Public Access to Your Workflow

The Minimum Material: Submit your core data frames and raw source code scripts as mandatory supplementary online files upon publication.
The Review Advantage: Exposing your full workspace infrastructure increases reviewer trust, accelerates editorial turnaround times, and boosts your project’s future citation metrics.
The Open Stance: Always remain prepared to openly answer peer requests for deep architectural or parameter pipeline metrics.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Screens Off, Minds On



Devices Away: Laptops & tablets closed, phones away.
No One Alone: Pair or team up (no solo seats).
Engage Fully: Be ready to speak, debate, and share ideas.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 1
Your teammate creates a breathtaking, beautifully styled bar chart for a group presentation. However, when the professor asks to see the 10,000 raw data points that generated the third bar, your teammate sweats and says, “Uh, it’s on my old laptop.”



Can a highly styled chart have any actual academic value?
How should losing access to raw files be treated?
Should the student be accused of data fabrication?





−+
04:00




A pretty chart without raw data trails isn’t science; it’s just creative writing/coding. There is not a lot of academic value in a breathtaking, highly styled chart if the baseline data supporting it cannot be produced on demand.
“The burden of proof.” In some professional environments, an inability to instantly back up a specific visual claim with its underlying numbers looks less like a mistake and more like data fabrication.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 2
A student keeps a beautiful, 100-page handwritten leather notebook. She tracks every single mouse click, every copy-paste action, and every manual data-cleaning step she performs in Excel with flawless precision.



Is the student’s work reproducible?
Is there any value in (or place for) hand-written notes?





−+
04:00




A beautifully kept manual record still fails the core requirement of being an “executable description” that a computer can run and scale.
Manual copy-paste actions and Excel mouse clicks introduce silent, untraceable human errors that version control cannot catch. We should prefer automated scripts that require zero human intervention to repeat.
There is immense value in handwritten notes and manual approaches, but only as a sandbox for human thought, not as the final pipeline for data execution.
The “Why” vs. the “How”: Code is excellent at tracking how a calculation is done, but it is terrible at explaining why you chose to do it. A handwritten notebook is a cognitive sandbox. It is where a researcher maps out messy conceptual logic, sketches potential workflows, and processes failures before writing a single line of script.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 3
You spend three weeks testing a hypothesis on a dataset. Your code is perfect, your pipeline is automated, but the results prove your hypothesis is completely, totally wrong. Your script yields a massive “dead end.”



Did your hypothesis fail, or did you?
Did you just waste 3 weeks of work?
Would you still share your work in a public repo?





−+
04:00





Did your hypothesis fail, or did you? It’s important to separate the quality of your code from the behavior of nature.
Also, an automated “failed” experiment is actually a massive engineering success.
Did you just waste 3 weeks of work? The danger of deleting your dead ends: What happens to the scientific community when researchers hide their failures, forcing the next person to waste weeks re-testing the exact same wrong idea.
Would you still share your work in a public repo? Submit and store it with the exact same reproducibility standards as a success, because documenting “blind alleys” saves future researchers from wasting time on the same mistake.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Scenario 4
Your script runs a 4-hour simulation on a large dataset, processing everything live in temporary memory to output a final summary paragraph. When your professor spots an anomaly and asks to see the data right after the initial filtering step, you realize nothing was saved along the way.



What are some advantages of a single “all-or-nothing” live run?
What are some disadvantages of saving intermediate steps?





−+
04:00




Disadvantages of a pipeline that only saves the final answer: impossible to troubleshoot, audit, or verify when a bug or anomaly inevitably appears in the middle.
Discuss the massive waste of time and computational energy that happens when you treat data analysis as a single “all-or-nothing” live run instead of caching milestones.
Debate the engineering trade-off between consuming hard drive space to store temporary milestone files versus consuming hours of processing time to re-run scripts.
Better to transform a 4-hour pipeline into a modular, flexible workflow that can be paused, inspected, and restarted at any point.

Poll
Be completely honest: When cleaning a dataset or fixing file formatting issues for an assignment, how often do you rely on manual copy-pasting, visual cell edits, or find-and-replace clicks instead of writing a code script?

100% Code Scripted: I never touch the raw file manually; every transformation is written in a reproducible script lines.
The Hybrid Scramble: I try to script, but if a deadline is tight, I secretly open Excel to quickly delete bad rows or copy-paste columns.
Purely Manual: I do almost all data formatting visually using trackpad movements and mouse clicks because it feels faster.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll

You notice a minor discrepancy in plot you generated 3 weeks ago. You need to backtrack to the exact code state that produced that specific figure.
What is the reality of your current local file system?


Perfect Provenance: Every single script modification is systematically frozen in a timestamped Git commit hash; I can jump back in seconds.
The “Folder Vault” Cluster I have copies named script_v1.R, script_v2_fixed.R, and script_final_REAL.R. It will take hours of manual guessing.
The Overwrite Abyss: I continuously modify a single file without saving historical backups. That past code state is permanently gone.
The Cloud Illusion: I assume my background Google Drive/Dropbox sync will save me, even though it doesn’t track execution states.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll
You run a classmate’s random simulation script on your machine using identical data inputs. But they forgot to set a static random seed. Your output values are approximately close (e.g., 84.2% accuracy) but not exactly equal to their published value (84.5%). What is your scientific verdict?

Acceptable Replication: Close enough is good enough for computational science; minor stochastic fluctuations don’t undermine the core theory.
Unverifiable Black Box: An approximate match is a failure; without an exact mathematical match via a random seed, I cannot verify if the pipeline is truly bug-free.
Indifferent Stance: I assume the difference is caused by our different operating system kernels or processor architectures anyway, so a seed won’t fix it.

title: 10 Simple Rules for RR
text:
Poll
Think about how you write lab reports, group notes, or draft research paragraphs. Where do your conceptual interpretations live relative to the raw output data files that support them?

Fully Welded Documents: I use integrated dynamic document tools (like Quarto or Jupyter Notebooks) so my text and live data logic are locked together natively.
The Absolute Path Blind Bind: I manually type hardcoded server folder paths (e.g., /Users/name/Desktop/run_3) inside a separate Microsoft Word document.
The Total Disconnect: My data lives in a folder on a local server, and my interpretations live entirely in casual emails, Slack chats, or scrap paper notes.

section: 1. Saving Multiple Versions of a File
text:
1. Saving Multiple Versions of a File

A student builds an amazing regression model at 2:00 AM. Exhausted, they save the code as model_final.py.


The next morning, they realize they missed an outlier, tweak the file, and save it as model_final_v2.py.


Two weeks later, their professor asks for a minor adjustment. They end up with model_final_revised_PROFCORRECTED.py.



When looking back at the folder a month later, they have no idea which file generated the actual metrics in their final presentation slide deck.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
2. Hardcoding Absolute Paths

Alex writes a brilliant data cleaning script on his Windows laptop.


He uploads it to a shared folder so his lab partner, Chloe, can run it on her MacBook.


The second Chloe hits execute, the terminal crashes with a fatal File Not Found Error.



The script failed instantly because Chloe’s computer doesn’t have a user named “Alex,” and Mac operating systems don’t even use a C:/ drive design.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
3. Polluting the Global Environment

Maria installs Pandas version 1.5 globally on her laptop to run a machine learning project for a class.


Next semester, she takes an advanced statistics class that requires a new feature only found in Pandas version 2.2. She runs a global upgrade command.



When she tries to re-run her old machine learning code for her portfolio, it completely crashes with syntax errors.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
4. Silent Corruptions

David notices that a few rows in his sensor log dataset contain a typo: "N/A" instead of blank spaces.


He opens the raw file in Microsoft Excel, uses “Find and Replace” to clean them up, hits save, and closes the window.


What he doesn’t realize is that Excel silently reformatted his entire Date column from standard YYYY-MM-DD strings into a localized format like MM/DD/YY, and dropped the leading zeros on all his zip codes.



His Python analysis script now breaks completely because the data was fundamentally altered by a silent software default.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
5. Out-of-Order Executions

Sam is actively prototyping a data chart:

He runs cell 1 to load data,
skips down to cell 10 to drop missing values,
runs cell 4 to alter a variable,
and then jumps back to cell 2 to plot the results.



The graph looks perfect. He saves the notebook and emails it to his professor.


The professor opens the file, hits “Run All Cells” from top to bottom, and gets an entirely different chart with a broken trendline.



The perfect result only existed because of the chaotic, invisible memory sequence trapped inside Sam’s live session.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
6. Dangers of Copy-Pasting

Elena computes a critical p-value for her research paper: 0.00412. She opens her jupyter notebook, and types it in.


Later that week, she realizes her input data had duplicated rows, so she runs the script again. The new correct p-value changes to 0.0412.


Because the report is a completely detached text file, she forgets to update the document manually.



She accidentally publishes a report with a massive typo that completely flips the statistical significance of her research.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
7. Unrepeatable Breakthroughs

A student builds a fraud-detection model that achieves an impressive 95% accuracy score.


Excitedly, she calls her supervisor over to show them the breakthrough. She hits execution again to demonstrate the live pipeline.


The accuracy drops to 89%. She runs it a third time, and it jumps to 92%.



Because she forgot to hardcode a random seed marker (numpy.random.seed(42)), the dataset splits randomly on every execution, rendering her breakthrough metrics entirely un-reproducible.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
8. The Interactive GUI Trap

Kevin uses a graphical enterprise software program to clean a dataset, clicking visual buttons to remove columns, drop null rows, and filter outliers.


He exports a beautiful chart for a corporate presentation.


Six months later, a regulatory compliance officer demands an audit trail detailing exactly why certain outlier rows were dropped from the dataset.



Because Kevin handled the entire process through manual mouse clicks inside a black-box GUI rather than writing a programmatic script, he has no way to prove or replicate his step-by-step logic, putting the validity of the entire project at risk.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
9. The Single-Commit Mega-Upload

Ryan works diligently on an assignment for three weeks without committing a single line of code.


On Sunday night, he runs git add . and git commit -m "fixed project stuff", pushing the entire thing to GitHub.


On Monday morning, his professor points out that a code adjustment made on day 4 accidentally ruined the data integrity pipeline.



Because Ryan mashed 21 days of complex, erratic file changes into a single history node, he cannot roll back the graph to isolate the error, forcing him to manually untangle his entire codebase.

title: Welcome to STAT 159-259
text:
10. The “Free Real Estate” Licensing Illusion

An open-source research team discovers a student’s public repository containing a clever, highly optimized data parsing code.


They want to integrate it into a medical framework that could save lives, but their legal compliance department blocks it completely.


Because the student forgot to include an explicit LICENSE file (like MIT or Apache 2.0), the code legally defaults to strict, restrictive copyright ownership.



The useful pipeline remains legally locked away from helping the community.

title: Git Branches
section: What Exactly is a Git Branch?
text:
What Exactly is a Git Branch?


A branch is NOT a heavy folder containing copies of your files.
A branch is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to a specific commit in your history graph.
Creating a branch is instantaneous and costs almost zero disk space. It just creates a 41-byte text file containing a commit hash.

title: Git Branches
text:
When to use branches?

Feature Development: Writing a new data cleaning function or engineering a new feature.
Experimentation: Testing a different model architecture (e.g., switching from a Random Forest to an XGBoost model).
Bug Fixes: Fixing an error in your data parsing script without pausing ongoing analysis.
Collaboration: Every team member works on their own branch, keeping the main branch stable, tested, and deployable at all times.

section: Traps and Confusing Things to Avoid
text:
Traps and Confusing Things to Avoid

Trap: Uncommitted changes
Description: If you edit a file but do not commit it, and then switch branches, those uncommitted changes travel with you to the new branch.
Rule: Always run git status and commit or stash1 changes before switching branches.

We’ll cover stashing later.

title: Git Branches
section: Traps and Confusing Things to Avoid

Description: Avoid naming branches like git branch test1.

title: Git Branches
section: Traps and Confusing Things to Avoid
text:
Traps and Confusing Things to Avoid

Trap: Losing Track of HEAD
Description: If you checkout a specific commit hash instead of a branch name, you enter a “Detached HEAD state”. Commits made here do not belong to any branch and can easily be lost.

title: Git Branches
text:
Merging

You can integrate the changes of a branch into another branch by merging these branches.
Afterwards, the commits of the new branch (e.g. “feature”) are also part of the main branch’s history.

title: Git Branches
text:
Types of Merges
2 main types of merges:


Fast-Forward Merge

Occurs if main hasn’t changed since you branched off.
Git simply slides the main pointer forward to match your feature branch pointer.
No new commit is made.


Three-Way Merge

Occurs if main has moved forward while you were working.
Git looks at the common ancestor, merges the differences.
Git creates a new Merge Commit node with two parent pointers.

title: Git Branches
text:
Fast-Forward Merge
If the base branch (main) has not received any new commits since you created the feature branch, Git completes the merge by simply moving the branch pointer forward to the latest commit of the feature branch.
No new “merge commit” is generated because there are no divergent changes to reconcile.

title: Git Branches
text:
Three-Way Merge
If both the feature branch and the main branch have moved forward independently with new commits, the history has diverged.
Git combines changes from two divergent branches and creates a special Merge Commit with two parent pointers.
The term “three-way” refers to the three snapshots Git compares to generate the merged file:

The Common Ancestor (Merge Base): The point in history where the two branches originally split. It acts as the baseline.
The Target Branch (HEAD): The tip (most recent commit) of the branch you are currently on and merging into.
The Source Branch: The tip of the branch you are actively trying to merge.

title: Git Branches
text:
Merge Conflicts

There can be conflicts when branches are merged.
A conflict happens when two branches modify the exact same line of the exact same file, and you try to merge them.
Git doesn’t know which version is the correct one.

title: Git Branches
text:
Resolving conflicts
The process of resolving a conflict is similar to the usual commit workflow:

Modify: Resolve all conflicts.
Add: Add all changes to the staging area via git add.
Commit: Conclude the conflict resolution and the merge operation via git commit.

title: Git Branches
text:
Merge Conflicts
Git pauses the merge, alters your file to show the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>), and forces you to manually edit and fix the code before committing.
INSERT IMAGE

title: Git Branches
text:
Strategies to reduce conflicts

Try to keep lines short (makes it easy to spot where the conflicts are).
Try to keep your commits small and focused.
Try to merge often. In this way, the conflicts will be smaller and more isolated.
The longer you wait to merge, it will be more likely to have bigger conflicts.
Track changes to main.

title: Git Branches
text:
Stashing
Imagine you are in the middle of writing a new feature, and your code is completely broken and full of typos.
Suddenly, your professor or project manager sends an urgent message: “The login screen is completely broken on the main server. Fix it right now.”
You can’t switch branches to fix the bug because Git won’t let you switch branches while you have dirty, uncommitted changes.
But you also don’t want to run git commit on broken, unfinished work just to save it.
This is where you run git stash

title: Git Branches
text:
How Stashing Works (The Workspace Analogy)
Think of your code folder like a messy physical desk full of scribbled-on scratch paper and unfinished blueprints:

git stash: You take all the messy papers on your desk, shove them into a drawer, and lock it. Your desk is now perfectly clean.
The Emergency Intermission: You safely switch branches, write a clean 1-line fix for the server bug, commit it, and push it.
git stash pop: You open the drawer, take your messy papers out, and spread them back out on your desk exactly where you left them. You can now resume your work as if you were never interrupted.

title: Git Branches
text:
Two Mistakes Beginners Make

Untracked Files: By default, git stash only saves files that Git already knows about. If you created a brand new file and haven’t run git add on it yet, Git will leave it sitting on your desk. To force Git to stash everything including new files, you must run: git stash -u (short for untracked).
The Stash Black Hole: If you run git stash five times over a week without using git stash pop, you will end up with a massive pile of nameless stashes. It becomes very difficult to remember what code is hidden inside stash@{4}.

About GNU Make

GNU Make, commonly known as make, is a Unix tool that is part of the GNU Project.
To work with Make you write a text file with the name Makefile, typically referred to as the makefile.
Notice that Makefile has not file extensions!

title: Intro to GNU Make (part 1)
text:
What’s in a Makefile?
A makefile is formed by rules that have the following structure:



Makefile

# rule
target: dependencies
  commands




A rule tells Make how to execute a series of commands in order to build a target file from source files (i.e. the dependencies).
⚠️ IMPORTANT: the recipe line(s) must be indented with a TAB and not with any spaces.

title: Intro to GNU Make (part 1)
text:
Basic rule syntax

Under its most basic form, a rule usually has this structure:


Makefile

# rule to generate target
target: dependency
  command




target is the output file
dependency is the input file
command is the program that creates the target
the command line is indented with a TAB

title: Intro to GNU Make (part 1)
text:
Phony Targets

By default, Makefile targets are file targets
This means that targets are used to build files from other files (i.e. the dependencies)
This implies that Make assumes the target of a rule is a file.
There are occasions, however, when a given target is not really a file, but simply the name of a recipe
The most common example is the all target

title: Intro to GNU Make (part 1)
text:
Phony target all

# all outputs

# rule 2: doc.pdf
doc.pdf: doc.qmd
  quarto render doc.qmd --to pdf


The first target all is not the name of a file;
It is simply a convenient “label” to indicate a series of dependencies.
This type of target is known in Make terminology as a phony target.
Phony meaning “not a real file”.

About

Example

title: R Packaging
text:
Building An R Package
Now that we have most of the common elements of an R package, let’s talk about the package-building process.
I will show the way I like to create my packages.
This means that you may find other useRs following different building strategies.

title: R Packaging
text:
Package States
The creation process of an R package can be done in several ways. Depending on the modus operandi that you choose to follow, it is possible for a package to exist in five different states:

Source
Bundled
Binary
Installed
In-memory

title: R Packaging
text: Package States

title: R Packaging
text:
Source Package






The starting point is always a source package.
This is basically the directory containing the subdirectories and files that form your package.
I like to think of this state as a package in a raw stage.
From a source package, you can transition to other states.

title: R Packaging
text:
Source Package






The next immediate state (although not mandatory) is a bundled package.
This involves wrapping the source package into a single compressed file.
The compressed file has the extension .tar.gz

A .tar, short for Tape ARchive or tarball, is a standard format in the Unix/Linux environment.
A .gz file is simply the type of compression.

title: R Packaging
text:
Binary Package






A package in binary form is another type of state for a package.
This is another type of compressed file that is platform specific.
This depends on the operating system you are working with:

Mac/Linux
Windows

title: R Packaging
text:
Installed Package






An installed package is a decompressed binary file that has been unwrapped into an actual package library.
Typically, it will be located in the directory where other package libraries are stored.

title: R Packaging
text:
In-memory Package






Lastly, in order to use an installed package you need to load it into memory.
This is done with the library() function.

title: R Packaging
text:
During the development of a package, you always start at the source level, and eventually make your way to an installed version.





In theory, the building process would consist of the following flow:
source -> bundle -> binary -> installed —> in-memory
In practice, however, you can take some detours and shortcuts from source to installed.

title: R Packaging
text:
Packaging Flow
A typical packaging workflow involves the following steps:

Create Documentation
Check Documentation
Run Tests
Build Bundle
Install Package
Check Package

title: R Packaging
text:
Packaging Flow
A typical packaging workflow involves the following steps:

Create Documentation:    devtools::document()
Check Documentation:    devtools::check_man()
Run Tests:    devtools::test()
Build Bundle:    devtools::build()
Install Package:    devtools::install()
Check Package:    devtools::check()

title: R Packaging
text:
Create Documentation
When you change the roxygen comments of your functions, you will need to (re)generate the corresponding manual documentation.


This can be done with the function devtools::document() which generates the so-called .Rd (R documentation) files, located in the man/ directory.

title: R Packaging
text:
Check Documentation
An optional—but strongly recommended—step after new documentation has been generated, is to check that it is correct.


This step becomes mandatory if you plan to share your package via CRAN.


To check that the .Rd files are okay, use the function
devtools::check_man() which inspects that the content and syntax of the .Rd files are correct.

title: R Packaging
text:
Run Tests
If your package contains unit-tests (strongly suggested), included in the directory tests/, you can use the function devtools::test() to run such tests.

title: R Packaging
text:
Build Bundle
If you just simply want to convert a package source into a single bundled file, you use the function devtools::build()


This function will create, by default, the .tar.gz file that in turn can be installed on any platform.


build() does not generate or check any documentation. It also does not run any tests.

title: R Packaging
text:
Install
To install the package you can use devtools::install()


This function can install a source, bundle or a binary package.


After the installation is done, you should be able to load the package with library() in order to use its functions, and inspect its manual documentation.

title: R Packaging
text:
Check
Optionally, you can carry out an integral check of the package with the function devtools::check()


This checking process is a comprehensive one, and it will verify pretty much every single detail.


This step also becomes mandatory if you plan to share your package via CRAN.

title: R Packaging
text:
Optional devtools file
Unless you are constantly creating packages, you will very likely forget what functions to use for a specific purpose. One small hack that I tend to use is to include an auxiliary .R file in the source package, which I typically name as devtools-flow.R (or something like that) with the following content:


devtools-flow.R

# Devtools workflow
devtools::load_all()   # load your functions (then try them out)
devtools::document()   # generate documentation
devtools::check_man()  # check documentation
devtools::test()       # run tests (if any)
devtools::build()      # build bundle
devtools::install()    # install package
devtools::check()      # comprehensive check (optional)

title: R Packaging
text:
Optional devtools file

You can think of devtools-flow.R as a cheat-sheet.
This file should be included in .Rbuildignore.
Add a new line with the name of the file to .Rbuildignore, and remember to anchor it with ^ and $.
Here’s what your .Rbuildignore file may look like:




.Rbuildignore

^average\.Rproj$
^\.Rproj\.user$
^\.positai$
^\.claude$
^data-raw$
^devtools-flow.R$

Goals
By the end of the course, students will:

understand the issues regarding reproducible research in modern scientific practice, including the definitions of key concepts and the different challenges that exist across disciplines
understand the computational and statistical issues involved with reproducibility
be proficient at the Unix commandline
be proficient at version control with Git

Format and assessment
This is an in-person class with three one-hour lectures each week and one two-hour lab led by a GSI.
Lectures will focus on theory, philosophy of science, foundations of statistics, scientific applications, software engineering, code reviews and group discussion.
Lab will focus on computing, software tools, workflow, and collaboration; a short and easy checkpoint on that lab’s material will occur each session. You must attend the lab section you are officially enrolled in. If this presents significant burden, please reach out to your lab TA.

Consistent class participation is crucial: we will be discussing subtle substantive, technical, and philosophical issues and reviewing code during class. If you cannot attend the lectures synchronously, please do not take the course.
You will be interacting with course staff and fellow students in several different environments: in class, in lab, over the discussion forum, and in office hours. Some of these will be in person, some of them will be online, but the same expectations hold: be kind, be respectful, be professional.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI Tools policy
We strongly encourage you to focus on independent learning and original problem-solving. At the same time, we recognize that generative AI tools are an increasingly standard part of modern workflows. We are not banning AI tools in this course, as doing so is neither realistic nor desirable.
This course is designed to help you build fundamental skills, judgment, and deep understanding—outcomes AI cannot achieve for you. Our main goal is to foster transparency and genuine engagement with the material, aligning with the core philosophy of STAT 159/259.
Core Expectations 

Do the thinking yourself. Use AI to support your learning, not replace it. If a tool handles the core reasoning, drafting, or problem-solving while you merely copy and submit the output, you are missing out on learning the material.
Disclose your usage. If you use AI tools on an assignment—whether for brainstorming, debugging code, editing text, checking work, or drafting—you must state so explicitly. A short note on your assignment is sufficient: include the tool and version used (e.g., Claude 3.5 Sonnet, ChatGPT-4o), what you used it for, the primary prompts used, and where it was applied.


Why this matters: Transparency aligns directly with the collaborative and reproducible data science practices central to this course. Openly documenting how work was produced ensures your workflow can be evaluated and built upon by others.


Understand everything you submit. You are fully accountable for all submitted work. If you include AI-generated code, text, or figures, you must be able to explain, defend, and walk through them as if you created them entirely yourself. If you cannot explain a line of code or a specific claim, do not submit it.
Violations of the course AI policy:

Undisclosed AI Use: Submitting AI-assisted or AI-generated work without clear disclosure.
Lack of Comprehension: Submitting AI-generated work that you cannot explain, defend, or demonstrate understanding of when asked.


The ultimate objective of this course isn’t just to produce correct answers; it is to build critical thinking, master modern tools, and communicate complex ideas clearly. Using AI responsibly and transparently is part of developing those professional skills.

The high academic standard at the University of California, Berkeley, is reflected in each degree awarded. Every student is expected to maintain this high standard by ensuring that all academic work reflects unique ideas or properly attributes the ideas to the original sources.

Accepted formats: PDF, HTML, MS Word (.docx), or Google Doc



1. Reflecting on Reproducible
The Turing Way defines a “reproducible” result as using the same data and the same analysis steps. Think back to a programming or data assignment you submitted in a previous semester.
If your laptop was lost today and you had to reconstruct that project on a classmate’s machine using only your memory and the files currently backed up in your email/cloud, what are the exact “ghosts” (a hidden file path, an unrecorded package version, an un-downloaded dataset) that would cause the reproduction to completely fail?


2. Reflecting on Robust
A result is “robust” if using different analysis steps on the same data yields a qualitatively identical answer (e.g., swapping from an R package to a Python script).
If you were forced to completely rewrite your favorite data script into a programming language you barely know, which specific part of your code’s logic do you suspect would fall apart or yield a different mathematical rounding result, and why?


3. Reproducible Failure
Imagine a peer creates a messy, un-versioned script that accidentally discovers a brilliant, groundbreaking pattern in a public dataset, but their workflow is completely un-reproducible.
You build a flawless, fully automated, version-controlled pipeline that proves a hypothesis is completely wrong, but anyone can rerun it perfectly. In your own words, defend why your “reproducible failure” might actually be more valuable to the progress of science than their “sloppy success.”

title: Project 2) Replicating Claims from 2024 BPD Annual Report
text:
2024 BPD Annual Report
Every year, the Berkeley Police Department (BPD) publishes an Annual Report to document their measurable progress, and to communicate their activities and achievements around five major topics:

Staffing & Workload
Crime & Investigations
Road Safety & Collisions
Stop Data
Use of Force

You can find the 2024 Berkeley Police Department Annual Report in the following link:
https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/BPD%202024%20Annual%20Report.pdf

Data Sets for Project 2
Some of the data collected by BPD is shared to the public through their so-called Transparency Hub: https://bpd-transparency-initiative-berkeleypd.hub.arcgis.com/. This is an online public data portal maintained by BPD to share near-real-time policing metrics, crime trends, and operational records.
For this assignment, we want you to focus on some of the claims reported in the sections “Road Safety & Collisions” and “Stop Data”. You can find the associated CSV data sets in the Data Portal tab of the Transparency Hub: https://bpd-transparency-initiative-berkeleypd.hub.arcgis.com/search

Collision Data (2011 to Current)
Berkeley PD Stop Data (2024 - Current)



Replication Targets
Here are the claims (e.g. numeric summaries, tables, graphics) from the 2024 BPD Annual Report that you will attempt to reproduce:

Table of “Collision Totals” (page 18)
Table of “Top collision locations” (page 19)
Bar chart of “Primary Collision Factors, 2024” (page 19)
Bar chart of “Most frequent vehicle violations, 2024” (page 21)

Temperature Anomalies
\[
\text{Temp Anomaly} = \text{Observed Temp} - \text{Baseline Average Temp}
\]

A temperature anomaly is a departure or deviation from a long-term average, baseline “normal” temperature.
Instead of measuring the absolute, raw temperature (e.g., “The temperature in Death Valley today is 45°C”), climate scientists measure how much warmer or colder a specific time and place is compared to its historic reference baseline.

title: Case Study: Global Temperature Anomalies
text:
Temperature Anomalies
\[
\text{Temp Anomaly} = \text{Observed Temp} - \text{Baseline Average Temp}
\]
What the Numbers Mean:

Positive Anomaly (+): The observed temperature was warmer than the historic baseline average.
Negative Anomaly (-): The observed temperature was cooler than the historic baseline average.
Zero Anomaly (0): The temperature was exactly equal to the long-term historical average.

title: Case Study: Global Temperature Anomalies
text:
Why Using Anomalies?

Why not just average absolute temperatures?
Absolute temperatures are heavily distorted by local geography.
e.g. If you have two weather stations—one at the bottom of a mountain and one at the peak—their absolute temperatures will vary wildly due to elevation.
While absolute temperatures shift from mile to mile, temperature anomalies are highly correlated across vast distances.
e.g. If a winter is unusually warm in Chicago, it is almost certainly unusually warm in Detroit, Milwaukee, and across the entire Midwest.
Because the anomaly signal is uniform across large regions, they accurately reflect temperature trends even in data-sparse areas.

Computers don’t care about comments, or style, or the naming of things. But users and collaborators (and yourself six months from now) will.

title: Writing Clear Code

text:
Writing functions

Break large tasks into small units.

Make each discrete unit a function.

If you write the same code more than once, make it a function.
If a line/block of code is complicated, make it a function.
Modularity is really important for readability.
No long streams of code; rather, a short set of function calls.

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Don’t Repeat Yourself (or others)

Avoid having repeated blocks of code.
Create functions, and call those functions repeatedly.
This is easier to maintain.

If something needs to be fixed/revised, you just have to do it the one time.

Look at others’ libraries/packages.

Don’t write what others have already written (especially if they’ve done it better that your would have)

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Don’t make things too specific

Write code that is a bit more general than your specific data

Don’t assume particular data dimensions.
Don’t forget about the possibility of missing values (even if your data doesn’t have any).
Aim for re-use.

Use function arguments

Don’t assume particular data file names
Don’t hard-code tuning parameters

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Avoid global variables!

Don’t refer directly to objects in your workspace.

Global variables make code unreadable.

If a function needs something, pass it as an argument.

Global variables make code difficult to reuse.

(But what about really big data sets?)


You shouldn’t be afraid to pass really big data sets into and between functions.

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
No magic numbers

Magic number, e.g.: 1000

You’ll later ask yourself “Why 1000?”

Name numbers and use the names

max_iter <- 1000
tol_convergence <- 0.0001

Even better: include them as function arguments

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Indent!

Don’t be afraid of indentation
Don’t underestimate indentation
Makes things clear, easier to read and inspect
