ggplot(mtcars,aes(x=disp,y=mpg,color=factor(cyl)))+geom_point(alpha=0.5,size=2)+geom_smooth(method="lm",se=FALSE)+



👍 Do
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = disp, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2)+
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

title: Writing Clear Code
Writing Clear Code
text:
Names: menaningful

Make names descriptive but concise
Avoid tmp1, tmp2, ...
Only use i, j, x, y in the simplest situations
If a function is named fv, what might it do?
If an object is called nms, what could it be?
Functions as verbs; objects as nouns

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Names

Sometimes it’s hard to come up with good names. But it’s really important.
Descriptive names make code self-documenting.
If functions are named by what they do, you may not need to explain further.
If the object names are meaningful, the code will be readable as it stands.
If the objects are named g, g2, and gg, it’ll need a lot of comments.
Finding/using good names may take time, but it pays off.

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Names: consistent

markers vs mnames
camelCase vs snake_case vs CapitalCase
nind vs n.var
If a function/object has one of these, there shouldn’t be an object/function with the other.

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Names: avoid confusion

Don’t use both total and totals
Don’t use both n.cluster and n.clusters
Don’t use both result and results
Don’t use both Mat and mat
Don’t use both g and gg
Don’t use similar but different names, in the same function or across functions.
It’s confusing, and it’s prone to bugs from mistyping.

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Comments

Comment the tricky bits and the major sections
Don’t belabor the obvious
Don’t comment bad code; rewrite it
Document the input/output and purpose, not the mechanics
Don’t contradict the code

this happens if you revise the code but don’t revise the related comments

Comment code as you are writing it (or before)
Plan to spend 1/4 of your time commenting

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Comments

Some things are tricky and deserve explanation, so that when you come back to it, you have a guide.
But in many cases, code can be rewritten to be clear and self-documenting.
Commenting takes time. And no one ever goes back and adds comments later. It’s another one of those “invest for the future” type of things.

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Error & Warning Messages

Explain what’s wrong (and where)

error("nrow(X) != nrow(Y)")

Suggest corrective action

"You need to first run calc.genoprob()."

Give details

"nrow(X) (", nrX, ") != nrow(Y) (", nrY, ")"

Don’t give error/warning messages that users won’t understand.

X'X is singular

Don’t let users do something stupid without warning
Include error checking even in personal code

title: Writing Clear Code
text:
Check data integrity

Check that the input is as expected, or give warnings/errors.
Write these in the first pass (though they’re dull).

You may not remember your assumptions later

These are useful for documenting the assumptions

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Vocabulary





Fork
Copying a repository from someone else’s GitHub account to your own GitHub account in the cloud. (A fork is essentially GitHub-to-GitHub).



Clone (git clone)
Downloading a repository from the cloud (GitHub) to your local computer.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Two main workflows




The Fork-and-Pull Model
Best for: Open-source projects, contributing to software you don’t own, or class assignments where students shouldn’t have write access to a master template repository.

The Shared Repository Model
Best for: Close-knit project teams, software development teams, or small group assignments where all members have collaborator (write) access to the same repository.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
What Is Forking on GitHub

A fork is a complete copy of someone else’s repository that gets created under your own GitHub account.
When you fork a repository, you get all the files, commit history, and branches from the original project.
The original repository remains untouched.
Your fork lives independently on your account, where you have full control to make changes, create branches, and experiment freely.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
An Analogy

Imagine you’re at a library and you find a cookbook you love.
You can’t write in the library’s copy.
But you can photocopy the entire book, take it home, and make all the notes and changes you want.
That’s exactly what forking does with code repositories.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
The Fork-and-Pull Model
Here’s a simple flow:

You typically fork first on GitHub
Then clone your fork to your local machine
You make changes in your local repo
Push changes to your fork
Optionally submit changes back to the original

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Why Developers Use Forks

Contributing to Open Source Projects

You fork the project,
Make your improvements in your fork,
Then propose your changes back to the original project through a pull request

Experimenting Without Risk

Perhaps you want to add a feature,
Try a different approach,
Or learn how it works by modifying it.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Why Developers Use Forks (cont’d)

Creating Your Own Version

You want to take a project in a different direction than the original maintainer
Maybe you need features they don’t want to add,
Or you want to customize it heavily for your own needs.





You can maintain it independently, adding whatever features you want.


This is completely acceptable in open-source development, as long as you respect the project’s license.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
section: How to Fork a Repository on GitHub
text:
How to Fork a Repository on GitHub
Say you found a useful project at github.com/username/awesome-project that you want to work with.

First, navigate to the GitHub repository you want to fork
Look for the Fork button in the upper-right corner, and click it.
GitHub will ask you where you want to fork the repository.
For most cases, select your personal account.
Click the Create fork button.
GitHub will copy the entire repository to your account.



You’ll notice the repository name now shows "YourUsername/awesome-project" with a note underneath saying "forked from username/awesome-project"

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Understanding the Fork Connection

Your fork maintains a link to the original repository, which GitHub calls the "upstream" repository. You can see this relationship on your fork’s main page.
This connection serves several purposes.

It allows you to fetch updates from the original project later (we’ll cover this in detail in an upcoming lesson).
It also enables you to submit pull requests back to the original project.

The original repository has no automatic connection to your fork.
The original maintainer won’t receive notifications when you fork their project (forking is a normal, expected activity on GitHub).

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
What Happens After You Forked
Your Fork Is Independent

Once forked, your repository is yours.
Changes you make don’t affect the original.
Changes made to the original don’t automatically appear in your fork.
You can delete your fork, make it private, or do whatever you want with it.


Contributing Back to the Original

The ultimate purpose of many forks is to contribute improvements back to the original project.
This happens through pull requests, which we’ll cover in lab.
However, not every fork leads to a pull request, and that’s fine.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Working with Your Forked Repository
Remember, forking creates the copy on GitHub, but you still need to clone it to your local machine to make changes.

Go to your forked repository on GitHub.
Click the green “Code” button and copy the URL.

It will look something like: https://github.com/YourUsername/awesome-project.git

Open your terminal and navigate to where you want to store the project.
Use the git clone command:


git clone git@github.com:YourUsername/awesome-project.git

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Making Changes to Your Fork
Working with a fork locally is identical to working with any other Git repository.
You use the same commands: git add, git commit, git push, and git pull.



Let’s say you want to fix a typo in the README file:



# Make changes to README.md using your text editor

# Stage the changes
git add README.md

# Commit with a clear message
git commit -m "Fix typo in installation instructions"

# Push to your fork on GitHub
git push origin main

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario: Contributing a Bug Fix

You discover the project at github.com/hansolo/simple-calculator.
You notice the division function doesn’t handle division by zero properly.
Step 1) Fork the repository on GitHub (i.e. get your own copy)
Step 2) Clone your fork locally


git clone https://github.com/YourUsername/simple-calculator.git
cd simple-calculator

Step 3) Create a branch for your fix



git switch -c fix-division-by-zero

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario: Contributing a Bug Fix

Step 4) Make your changes

Edit calculator.py to add zero-check
Test the changes locally

Step 5) Commit and push


git add calculator.py
git commit -m "Add division by zero error handling"
git push origin fix-division-by-zero

Now your fork on GitHub has a branch with your bug fix. The original project still doesn’t have your changes—that’s where pull requests come in, which we’ll cover in lab.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Keep Your Fork Updated

The original repository will continue to receive updates after you fork it.
Your fork doesn’t automatically stay in sync.
Outdated forks can lead to conflicts when you try to contribute changes back.
Make it a habit to check for updates before starting new work in your fork.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Fork Only When Needed

There’s no limit to how many repositories you can fork on GitHub.
However, you should only fork repositories you actually plan to work with.
Don’t fork every interesting repository you find.
Forking is meant for repositories you plan to work with actively, not for bookmarking or showing support.
Use GitHub’s ⭐️ Star feature to bookmark repositories you find interesting.
Too many inactive forks clutter your profile and make it harder to manage your actual work.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Respect the License

When you fork a repository, you must respect its license.
The license tells you what you can and cannot do with the code.
Some licenses require you to keep the same license if you distribute your fork.
Always read the LICENSE file in the repository.
If there’s no license, technically you don’t have permission to use the code, even though it’s public on GitHub.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Cannot Push to Original Repository

When you clone your fork, the remote is automatically set correctly, and you can push changes to it. Use git remote -v to verify.
If you try to push directly to the original repository URL, you’ll get a permission denied error.
This is expected: you don’t have write access to repositories you don’t own.
If you accidentally cloned the original repository instead of your fork, you’ll need to change the remote URL or clone your fork instead.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Key Takeaways

Forking is a fundamental GitHub feature that enables safe experimentation and collaboration.
A fork creates a complete copy of a repository under your account, where you have full control.
You fork on GitHub, then clone your fork locally to work on it.
Changes you make stay in your fork until you decide to contribute them back through a pull request.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Shared Repository Workflow
1) Clone (Once): Every team member clones the same central repository directly:
git clone https://github.com/organization/shared-repo.git



2) Branch (Every time you code): Always create a new branch for your specific task. Never code directly on main:
git switch -c fix-typos




3) Push to Central Remote: Push your branch up to the shared repository:
git push origin fix-typos

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Shared Repository Workflow (cont’d)
4) Open a Pull Request (PR): Go to the shared GitHub repository. Open a Pull Request from fix-typos into main.



5) Code Review & Merge: Teammates review the PR, discuss changes, and click Merge once approved. Other team members then pull the updated main branch locally (git pull origin main).

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
What is a Pull Request?

A pull request (often called a PR) is a request to merge changes from one branch into another.
It’s not a Git feature, it’s a GitHub feature that makes collaboration easier and safer.
When you create a pull request, you’re saying:



“Here are my changes. Can we discuss them and merge them into the main branch if they look good?”

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Why use pull requests?

Code Review and Quality

Pull requests create a formal code review process.
Before your changes merge, teammates can review your code, spot bugs, suggest improvements, and share knowledge.

Discussion and Collaboration

Pull requests provide a dedicated space to discuss changes.
You can leave comments on specific lines of code, ask questions, explain your approach, and collaborate on solutions.
This keeps all conversation about a feature or fix in one place.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Why use pull requests? (cont’d)

Documentation of Changes

Each pull request documents what changed, why it changed, and who approved it.
This creates a historical record for understanding project evolution.

Testing Before Merging

Pull requests give you a chance to test changes in isolation before they affect the main branch.
Many teams run automated tests when a pull request is created.
If tests fail, you can fix the issues before merging.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
The Typical Pull Request Workflow

Create a new branch for your feature or fix
Make changes and commit them to your branch
Push your branch to GitHub
Open a pull request on GitHub
Team members review and discuss your changes
Make additional commits if changes are requested
Once approved, merge the pull request
Delete the feature branch

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Pull Request vs Direct Merge

You could technically merge branches directly using git merge on your local machine and push to the remote.
But pull requests add a layer of review and discussion that direct merges don’t provide.
Pull requests give your team a chance to review code, ask questions, suggest changes, and ensure everything works before merging.
This prevents bugs and maintains code quality.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Where Pull Requests Live

Pull requests exist on GitHub (or similar platforms like GitLab or Bitbucket), not in Git itself.
They’re a web-based feature that wraps around Git’s merge functionality.
This means you create, review, and manage pull requests through GitHub’s website or mobile app, not through Git commands in your terminal.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Anatomy of a Pull Request
A pull request page has several tabs and sections, each serving a different purpose.

Conversation Tab (i.e. Discussion)
Commits Tab (i.e. History)
Files Changed Tab (i.e. Diff view)

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario

# Start from main branch
git switch main
git pull origin main

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario

# Start from main branch
git switch main
git pull origin main

# Create feature branch
git switch -c add-contact-page

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario

# Start from main branch
git switch main
git pull origin main

# Create feature branch
git switch -c add-contact-page

# Create the contact page file
echo "<h1>Contact Us</h1>" > contact.html

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario

# Start from main branch
git switch main
git pull origin main

# Create feature branch
git switch -c add-contact-page

# Create the contact page file
echo "<h1>Contact Us</h1>" > contact.html

# Stage and commit
git add contact.html
git commit -m "Add contact page with basic heading"

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Scenario

# Start from main branch
git switch main
git pull origin main

# Create feature branch
git switch -c add-contact-page

# Create the contact page file
echo "<h1>Contact Us</h1>" > contact.html

# Stage and commit
git add contact.html
git commit -m "Add contact page with basic heading"

# Push to GitHub
git push origin add-contact-page



Now your branch is on GitHub, ready for a pull request.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Creating the PR on GitHub
On GitHub, you click “Compare & pull request” and fill out the form:

Title: Add contact page
Description: “This PR adds a new contact page to the website. The page includes a heading and will be expanded with a form in future work. Ready for review.”



You click “Create pull request”, and now your teammates can review it.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Review and Feedback
A teammate reviews your PR and comments:

“Looks good! Can you also add a paragraph explaining how to reach us?”




You make the change locally:

# Still on add-contact-page branch
echo "<p>Send us an email at hello@example.com</p>" >> contact.html

git add contact.html
git commit -m "Add contact email paragraph"

git push origin add-contact-page



The new commit automatically appears in the pull request.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Approval
Assuming everything is good, your teammate approves, and you merge the PR through GitHub’s interface.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Keep Pull Requests Small

Small pull requests are easier to review and less likely to have bugs.
Try to keep PRs focused on one feature or fix.
A 50-line change is much easier to review thoroughly than a 500-line change. Reviewers can give better feedback when they’re not overwhelmed.
If your change is large, consider breaking it into multiple smaller pull requests.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Write Clear Descriptions

Explain what you changed and why.
Don’t assume reviewers know the full context; give them the information they need.
Include:

screenshots for visual changes,
testing steps for new features,
and explanations for complex logic.

A good description speeds up review and prevents misunderstandings.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Respond to Feedback

When reviewers leave comments, respond to them.
Either make the suggested changes or explain why you took a different approach.
Mark conversations as resolved when you’ve addressed them. This keeps the pull request organized and shows what still needs attention.
Be open to feedback.
Code review makes everyone better at their craft.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Test Before Requesting Review

Make sure your changes work before asking for review.
Run the code, test edge cases, and verify nothing broke.
Reviewers should focus on code quality and design, not catching basic bugs you could have found yourself.
Respect your teammates’ time by submitting quality work.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Bug Fix Pull Requests

Bug fixes are usually small, focused PRs.
Create a branch, fix the bug, add a test if possible, and open a PR.
In your description, explain what the bug was, how to reproduce it, and how your fix solves it.
Bug fix PRs often get reviewed and merged quickly since they solve immediate problems.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Feature Pull Requests

New features are typically larger PRs.
Break big features into smaller PRs if possible,

perhaps one PR for the database changes
and another for the user interface.

Describe the feature’s purpose, how it works, and how to test it.
Include screenshots or videos for visual features.
Feature PRs often need more discussion and iteration than bug fixes.

title: Collaboration in GitHub
text:
Documentation Pull Requests

Documentation changes are just as important as code changes.
Fixing typos, improving explanations, or adding examples all deserve pull requests.
Documentation PRs are often quick to review since they’re usually straightforward.
They’re also a great way for beginners to contribute to projects.
Good documentation makes projects more accessible to everyone.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Undoing Changes
In these slides we’ll cover:

Undoing changes before committing

git restore

Amending the most recent commit

git amend

Undoing commits

git revert
git reset

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
When you modify a file …

It starts in your working directory as “modified.”




When you run git add, it moves to the staging area as “staged.”




Finally, when you run git commit -m "...", it gets saved to the repository as “committed.”

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
git restore

Sometimes you modify a file and realize you want to throw away those changes completely.
Maybe you experimented with code that didn’t work, or you accidentally deleted important lines.
The git restore command is the modern way to discard changes in your working directory.
It reverts the file back to how it looked in the last commit.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Using git restore
Let’s say you modified a file called eda.ipynb but want to discard all changes. Here’s how you check the status first:

git status


You might see output like this:
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   eda.ipynb


Now discard the changes:
git restore eda.ipynb





This command replaces eda.ipynb in your working directory with the version from the last commit. All your modifications disappear permanently, so use this carefully.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Restoring Multiple Files
You can restore several files at once by listing them:
git restore eda.ipynb styles.css index.html



Or restore all modified files in the current directory:
git restore .

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Unstaging Files from Staging Area

What if you already ran git add but now want to unstage a file?
You’re not trying to discard the changes—you just want to remove the file from the staging area.
This is like removing items from your shopping cart before checkout. The items (your changes) still exist, but they’re no longer queued for the next commit.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Using git restore --staged
The --staged flag tells Git to unstage a file:
git restore --staged eda.ipynb

After running this, eda.ipynb returns to the “modified” state.
Your changes remain intact in the working directory—they’re just no longer staged.


Check the status to confirm:
git status
You’ll see:
Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   eda.ipynb

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Unstaging All Files
To unstage everything at once:
git restore --staged .



This is helpful when you accidentally staged too many files and want to be more selective about what goes into your next commit.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
The Older git reset Method
Before Git 2.23, developers used git reset to unstage files:
git reset HEAD eda.ipynb



This command still works perfectly, and you’ll encounter it in many existing projects.
HEAD refers to your current commit, and this command says “unstage this file, but keep my changes.”

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Combining Unstaging and Discarding

Sometimes you want to both unstage a file and discard the changes. You can do this in two steps:


# Step 1: Unstage the file
git restore --staged eda.ipynb

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Combining Unstaging and Discarding
Sometimes you want to both unstage a file and discard the changes. You can do this in two steps:
# Step 1: Unstage the file
git restore --staged eda.ipynb

# Step 2: Discard the changes
git restore eda.ipynb



Think of it like taking an item out of your shopping cart and then deciding whether to put it back on the shelf or keep looking at it.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Checking Before You Undo
Before you discard changes, it’s smart to review what you’re about to lose. Git gives you tools to inspect your modifications.





Viewing Unstaged Changes
See exactly what changed in your working directory:
git diff

This shows line-by-line differences. If you see something important, you might decide not to undo it.


Viewing Staged Changes
Check what’s currently staged for commit:
git diff --staged

This helps you verify what will be included in your next commit before you unstage anything.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Safety Tips and Best Practices
Undoing changes is powerful, but it can be destructive. Here are some guidelines to work safely.

Always run git status before undoing anything. This shows you exactly what state your files are in and helps you choose the right command.
Use git diff to review changes before discarding them. Once you run git restore, those changes are gone forever—they’re not saved anywhere.
Be extra careful with git restore . because it affects all files at once. Consider restoring files one at a time when you’re learning.
If you’re unsure, you can always make a quick backup copy of your file outside Git before running any restore commands.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Scenario 1: Modified Wrong File
You edited slides.qmd by mistake and want to undo everything:

# Check what changed
git status

# Discard all changes to slides.qmd
git restore slides.qmd

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Scenario 2: Staged Too Many Files
You ran git add . but only wanted to stage app.R, not test.R:

# Unstage test.R only
git restore --staged test.R

# Now only app.R remains staged
git status

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Scenario 3: Want Fresh Start
You made many changes across multiple files and want to start over completely:

# Unstage everything
git restore --staged .

# Discard all changes
git restore .

# Verify clean state
git status

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Scenario 4: Practical Workflow
You modify index.html, styles.css, and app.R. Then you stage everything:
git add .

After reviewing, you realize app.R has experimental code that isn’t ready. You want to unstage it:
git restore --staged app.R


Now you look at the changes in app.R and decide they’re not worth keeping:
git restore app.R


Finally, you commit only index.html and styles.css:
git commit -m "Update homepage layout and styling"

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Amending a commit

Amending a commit means modifying the most recent commit you made.
You can change the commit message,
You can add forgotten files,
You can remove files you didn’t mean to include.


Note that:

When you amend, Git doesn’t actually edit the existing commit.
The original commit is discarded and replaced with the amended version.
This works perfectly when you’re working alone or haven’t shared your commits yet.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Changing the Last Commit Message
Imagine you just committed with a message that says "Fix bug" but you want something more descriptive like "Fix bug in slider widget".

Here’s how you do it.
# First, make your commit (let's say with a typo)
git commit -m "Fix bug in sdiler wigdet"

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Changing the Last Commit Message
Imagine you just committed with a message that says "Fix bug" but you want something more descriptive like "Fix bug in slider widget".
Here’s how you do it.
# First, make your commit (let's say with a typo)
git commit -m "Fix bug in sdiler wigdet"

# Oops! Notice the typo "sdiler wigdet"
# Amend it immediately:
git commit --amend -m "Fix bug in slider widget"

When you run this command, Git replaces your last commit with a new one that has the corrected message. The files and changes remain exactly the same—only the message changes.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
section: Adding Forgotten Files to the Last Commit
text:
Adding Forgotten Files to the Last Commit
Another common scenario is forgetting to include a file in your commit. Maybe you fixed a bug across two files but only staged one of them.

# You made a commit but forgot to include functions.py
git commit -m "Update data cleaning script"

title: Undoing Changes in Git
section: Adding Forgotten Files to the Last Commit
text:
Adding Forgotten Files to the Last Commit
Another common scenario is forgetting to include a file in your commit. Maybe you fixed a bug across two files but only staged one of them.
# You made a commit but forgot to include functions.py
git commit -m "Update data cleaning script"

# Realize you forgot functions.py
# Stage the forgotten file
git add functions.py

# Amend the previous commit to include it
git commit --amend --no-edit


The --no-edit flag tells Git to keep the same commit message. This is perfect when you only want to add files without changing the message.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Example with Message Change
You can also add files and change the message at the same time. This gives you complete control over fixing your commit.

# Original commit
git commit -m "Add new feature to dashboard"

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Example with Message Change
You can also add files and change the message at the same time. This gives you complete control over fixing your commit.
# Original commit
git commit -m "Add new feature to dashboard"

# Stage additional files
git add logo.png
git add dashboard.qmd

# Amend with new message
git commit --amend -m "Add logo to dashboard"

title: Undoing Changes in Git
section: Removing Files from the Last Commit
text:
Removing Files from the Last Commit
Sometimes you accidentally include files that shouldn’t be in a commit. Maybe you staged all changes with git add . and included an image file or temporary notes.

# You committed but included screenshot.png by mistake
git commit -m "Univariate summary statistics"

title: Undoing Changes in Git
section: Removing Files from the Last Commit
text:
Removing Files from the Last Commit
Sometimes you accidentally include files that shouldn’t be in a commit. Maybe you staged all changes with git add . and included an image file or temporary notes.
# You committed but included screenshot.png by mistake
git commit -m "Univariate summary statistics"

# Remove screenshot.png from the staging area
git restore --staged screenshot.png

# Amend the commit without that file
git commit --amend --no-edit


The file still exists in your working directory—it just won’t be part of this commit anymore. You can decide later whether to delete it or add it to your .gitignore file.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
⚠️ Dangers of Amending Pushed Commits

If you’ve already pushed your commit to GitHub or another remote repository, amending it creates major problems.




When you amend a pushed commit and try to push again, Git will reject your push. This happens because the histories have diverged—your local version doesn’t match the remote version.




Follow this simple rule: only amend commits that you haven’t pushed yet. Once you push, create a new commit to fix mistakes instead.


You might be tempted to use git push --force to override the remote. While this works technically, it causes serious issues for anyone who already pulled your original commit. Their history will conflict with the new one.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Undoing Commits

Sometimes you accidentally commit the wrong code and need to undo it.
Git offers two main ways to undo commits:

git revert
git reset

They both undo changes, but they work in completely different ways.

git revert creates a new commit that undoes previous work.
git reset rewrites your commit history.

Choosing the wrong command can cause problems, especially when working with others.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
git revert

git revert creates a new commit that undoes the changes from a previous commit.
It’s the safe option because it doesn’t delete or modify existing commits.
Instead, it adds a new commit that reverses the changes.
This approach is perfect when you’ve already pushed your commits to a remote repository and other people might be using them.
You’re not rewriting history; you’re adding to it.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
How git revert works
Suppose you have a file called dashboard.qmd and you’ve made several commits. Your commit history looks like this:


commit abc123 (HEAD -> main)
Date: Today

    Add new feature to tab 1

commit bcd456
Date: Yesterday

    Split layout into 2 tabs

commit cde789
Date: 2 days ago

    Initial commit

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
How git revert works

Now you realize the "Add new feature to tab 1" commit (abc123) introduced a problem.
You want to undo it, but you’ve already pushed it to GitHub and your teammate has pulled the changes.
Here’s how you use git revert:


# Revert the most recent commit
git revert HEAD

# Git will open your editor for a commit message
# The default message will be something like:
# "Revert 'Add new feature to tab 1'"

# Save and close the editor

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
How git revert works
After running git revert HEAD, Git creates a new commit that undoes the changes from abc123.

Your history now looks like this:

commit fed987 (HEAD -> main)
Date: Today

    Revert "Add new feature to tab 1"
    
commit abc123
Date: Today

    Add new feature to tab 1

commit bcd456
Date: Yesterday

    Split layout into 2 tabs




Notice that the original commit (abc123) is still there. The new commit (fed987) simply reverses its changes. This is safe and transparent.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Reverting Older Commits

You can also revert commits that aren’t at the top of your history. You just need to specify the commit hash:


# Revert a specific commit by its hash
git revert def456

# This creates a new commit that undoes the changes from def456




If the changes conflict with more recent commits, Git will ask you to resolve the conflicts manually.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Reverting Multiple (consecutive) Commits

You can revert multiple commits at once.
For example, say you want to revert the last 2 commits. Here’s how to do it.


# Revert the last 2 commits
# This creates 2 separate revert commits
git revert HEAD~2..HEAD
This creates new commits that undo the changes made in the last two commits on your current branch

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Reverting Multiple (consecutive) Commits

You can revert multiple commits at once.
For example, say you want to revert the last 2 commits. Here’s how to do it.

# Revert the last 2 commits
# This creates 2 separate revert commits
git revert HEAD~2..HEAD

# Or revert without creating commits immediately
# (you'll commit manually after)
git revert --no-commit HEAD~2..HEAD
git commit -m "Revert last two changes"

The --no-commit option is useful when you want to revert several commits but create only one revert commit instead of multiple ones.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Reverting Multiple (consecutive) Commits
git revert HEAD~2..HEAD

HEAD: Refers to the tip of your current branch (the latest commit).
HEAD~2: Refers to the commit two steps back from the top of your branch.
..: Specifies a range of commits (from HEAD~2 up to HEAD)
In Git range syntax A..B, A is exclusive and B is inclusive.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
When to use git revert
Use git revert in these situations:

You’ve already pushed your commits to a remote repository
Other people are working on the same branch
You want to maintain a clear history of what went wrong and how you fixed it
You’re working on a public repository where transparency matters
You need to undo a commit that’s several commits back in history



Revert is the professional choice for team environments. It shows accountability and keeps everyone’s work synchronized.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
What is git reset

git reset moves your branch pointer to a different commit, effectively removing commits from your history.
Unlike git revert, it doesn’t create new commits.
git reset simply pretends certain commits never happened.
This is powerful but dangerous, especially if you’ve already shared your commits with others.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
How git reset Works
Using the same example from before, suppose you want to completely remove the "Add new feature to tab 1" commit as if it never existed:

# Move HEAD back one commit (default is --mixed)
git reset HEAD~1


Your commit history now looks like:

commit bcd456 (HEAD -> main)
Date: Yesterday

    Split layout into 2 tabs

commit cde789
Date: 2 days ago

    Initial commit




The abc123 commit is gone from your history. This approach rewrites history. The commit no longer exists in your branch’s timeline.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
section: The tricky part about Git Reset: its modes
text:
The tricky part about Git Reset: its modes

git reset moves your current branch pointer backward to a previous commit.
But unlike a simple undo, reset gives you control over what happens to your changes:

Do you want to keep them both in working directory and staging area?
Do you want to keep them only in working directory?
Do you want to discard them?

Git offers three different reset modes:

--soft
--mixed
--hard

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
When Reset Causes Problems

If you’ve already pushed the commit you’re resetting, you’ll create a mess:


# You reset and try to push
git reset HEAD~1
git push origin main

# Error: Updates were rejected
# Your local branch is behind the remote

Git refuses to push because you’re trying to rewrite history that others might depend on.
This is why reset should only be used for commits that haven’t been shared yet.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
When to use git reset
Use git reset in these situations:

You made commits locally but haven’t pushed them yet
You’re working on a personal branch that no one else uses
You want to combine multiple commits into one (before pushing)
You accidentally committed something you want to completely remove
You want to restart your work from an earlier point



Reset is perfect for cleaning up your local work before sharing it with others. It’s like being able to edit your draft before publishing.

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Revert -vs- Reset


git revert

Creates a new commit that undoes changes
Increases the commit count (adds revert commits)
Preserves all commits, adds new ones
Safe for shared/public commits
Use it after pushing to remote
Team-friendly, transparent
Can be reverted again if needed


git reset

Moves branch pointer backward, removing commits
Decreases the commit count (removes commits)
Rewrites history by removing commits
Dangerous for shared commits
Use it before pushing
Can cause conflicts with teammates
Requires reflog to recover lost commits

title: Undoing Changes in Git
text:
Decide which command to use:

Have you pushed the commit to a remote repository?

Yes \(\rightarrow\) Use git revert
No \(\rightarrow\) Continue to question 2

Is anyone else working on this branch?

Yes \(\rightarrow\) Use git revert
No \(\rightarrow\) Continue to question 3

Do you want to keep the commit in history?

Yes \(\rightarrow\) Use git revert
No \(\rightarrow\) Use git reset



When in doubt, git revert is the safer choice. It might create a longer history, but it won’t cause problems for you or your teammates.

It takes care of allocating time and memory to programs.
It does very fundamental root level management.

Example: What happens when you create a folder?
Command like mkdir Photos

The Shell’s Job: You type mkdir Photos into your terminal. The shell reads this text, realizes you want to run the “make directory” program, and translates your request into a standard system request (a system call).
The Handshake: The shell passes this request across the boundary to the kernel.
The Kernel’s Job: The kernel receives the request. It checks if you have permission to modify the storage. It then talks directly to your Hard Drive or SSD, physically carving out space on the disk to save your new “Photos” folder.

title: UNIX Part 1
text:

The Operating System is the entire restaurant.
The Shell is the waiter. It takes your order (commands) and translates it.
The Kernel is the kitchen staff. They actually handle the raw ingredients (hardware, memory) and cook the food.
Notice: The waiter doesn’t talk to “the restaurant”—the waiter talks to the kitchen.

Title: Seven Easy Steps to Open Science (An annotated reading list)
Authors: Sophia Cruwell et al.
Journal: Zeitschrift fur Psychologie, 227(4), 237-248
Year: 2019
https://doi.org/10.1027/2151-2604/a000387

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 1: Open Science Core Concepts
Open Science is an umbrella movement encompassing

transparency,
rigor,
reproducibility, and
accessibility,

across the entire research lifecycle.

🌐 Step 1: Open Science (Understanding the Concept)

The Baseline Definition: It is the explicit process of making both the content and the entire process of producing scientific evidence transparent and accessible to others [INDEX].
The Reproducibility Standard: You must guarantee that an independent researcher can take your exact data and code, run the same analysis, and obtain identical results [INDEX].
The Replicability Standard: Your documentation must be clear enough that repeating your exact procedures with new participants yields the same findings [INDEX].
Targeting Human Bias: It serves as a necessary procedural defense wall against human cognitive biases, such as confirmation bias and post hoc self-deception [INDEX].
Shifting Career Metrics: Adopting these behaviors helps shift institutional hiring, funding, and promotion models away from shallow journal impact factors toward transparent metrics [INDEX].

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 2: Open Access (OA)
🟡 The Gold Route

Free for readers: anyone can read, download, print, and share the final published paper
Immediate Access: article is open right away on the day it is published
Open Licensing: Articles are usually published under open licenses
Author Choice: Authors can publish either in fully open-access journals or in hybrid journals
Article Processing Charge (APC): publishers often charge an author fee (APC)

APCs are typically paid by funds, grants
Some publishers offer fee waivers (e.g. researchers from low-income)

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 2: Open Access (OA)
🟢 The Green Route

Free for readers: anyone can read, download, print, and share the final published paper
Free for Authors: authors do not pay an Article Processing Charge (APC)
Self-archive: Authors have to archive/store their work themselves

You usually cannot upload the publisher’s final formatted PDF

Embargo Periods: Publishers often require a waiting period (e.g. 6-24 months) before self-archive copy is made public


🔓 Step 2: Open Access (Disseminating Research)

The Main Objective: Removing all systemic and economic barriers to accessing, distributing, and re-using published scientific findings online [INDEX].
The Gold Route: Publishing your work in an exclusively open-access or hybrid journal where it is made instantly free to the public by the publisher [INDEX].
The Green Route: Self-archiving your work for free by uploading your peer-reviewed manuscripts or preprints to public, stable repositories (e.g., PsyArXiv) [INDEX].
The Citation Advantage: Open-access articles receive a significant boost in professional utility, tracking between a 36% and 600% increase in citations [INDEX].
Enabling Meta-Research: Exposing plain text openly allows data scientists to use automated text- and data-mining tools to audit field-wide claims [INDEX].

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 3: Open Data, Materials, & Code


The F.A.I.R. Ingestion Pipeline

Findable: Permanent DOI assignment (e.g., via OSF)
Accessible: Unrestricted cloud repository locations
Interoperable: Non-proprietary formats (use .csv, not .xlsx)
Reusable: Comprehensive documentation and read-me file tracking


📊 Step 3: Open Data, Materials, and Code (Transparency Fundamentals)

The Minimal Baseline: Moving away from “trusting” a scientist’s written summary to instead making the raw data files behind the analysis completely public [INDEX].
Sharing Materials: Providing every document, experimental task, presentation tool, and digital stimulus required to reconstruct the exact study timeline [INDEX].
The FAIR Data Protocol: Ensuring that your shared assets are structured to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable over long periods [INDEX].
The Documentation Imperative: Writing detailed read-me files so that outside users (and your own future self) can understand your columns and file paths [INDEX].
Anonymization & Exceptions: Safeguarding participant privacy through careful data scrubbing, or explicitly reporting clear ethical boundaries when data cannot be shared [INDEX].

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 4: Reproducible Analyses
Structuring workflows so that independent researchers (or the original authors at a later date) can rerun the analysis code on the raw data and produce identical quantitative results.
Emphasizes computational reproducibility through scripted, programmatic analysis tools (such as R or Python), dynamic document generation (e.g., R Markdown, Quarto, Jupyter Notebooks), version control, and clear software environment specifications.

💻 Step 4: Reproducible Analyses (Scientific Computing Skillsets)

Computing as a Core Skill: Treating computing best practices as just as integral to high-quality science as fundamental laboratory techniques [INDEX].
The Raw Data Sanctuary: Saving your raw, untouched data files completely separate from any cleaned, manipulated, or transformed versions [INDEX].
Structural Project Folders: Dedicating a single isolated directory to each research project, with clear sub-directories for raw data, processed data, and text [INDEX].
Recording Processing Steps: Tracking every single step of data cleaning and analysis by coding your pipeline in open-source languages (like R or Python) [INDEX].
Stable DOI Archiving: Uploading your code scripts and research products to reputable, permanent, DOI-issuing repositories like Figshare, Dryad, or Zenodo [INDEX].

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 5: Preregistration & Registered Reports
Distinguishing between exploratory (hypothesis-generating) and confirmatory (hypothesis-testing) research to prevent post-hoc changes to study designs or analysis plans.

Pre-Data Lock: Committing to hypotheses and statistical plans before gathering or viewing data files.
Registered Reports: Submitting your study design to a journal for peer-review prior to data collection.
In-Principle Acceptance: The journal guarantees publication based on design rigor, completely regardless of the final outcome.


⏱️ Step 5: Preregistration and Registered Reports (Constraining Flexibility)

The Pre-Data Mandate: Committing to your hypotheses, study designs, and statistical analysis plans before you gather data or view the files [INDEX].
Demarcating Exploration: Forcing a transparent, unalterable boundary between planned confirmatory testing and unplanned, post hoc exploratory data mining [INDEX].
The Target Failure: Restricting a researcher’s degrees of freedom to eliminate HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) and cherry-picking [INDEX].
The Registered Report Pivot: Submitting your study design to a journal for pre-data peer-review to secure an “in-principle acceptance” before execution [INDEX].
The Stage 2 Audit: Guaranteeing publication based purely on the rigor of the design and adherence to the plan, completely regardless of whether the final results are positive [INDEX].

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 6: Replication Research
Conducting and publishing direct or conceptual replications to test the robustness and generalizability of existing empirical findings.
Replications are essential for building a cumulative, self-correcting science.

🔬 Step 6: Replication Research (Verifying Scientific Discoveries)

The Benchmark of Truth: Adopting the foundational scientific rule that an effect must be completely repeatable to count as a genuine scientific discovery [INDEX].
Direct Replications: Intentionally duplicating every necessary element of an original study to see if the physical result can be reproduced [INDEX].
Conceptual Replications: Purposefully changing operational components (like the measure or the sample) to evaluate the generalizability of the theory [INDEX].
The “Alternative Test” Label: Re-labeling messy conceptual replications as “alternative tests” to stop them from being conflated with close, direct replications [INDEX].
Systemic Stabilization: Embracing replication to fix structural market misalignments where fields reward novelty over long-term theory stability [INDEX].

title: 7 Steps to Open Science
text:
Step 7: Teaching Open Science
Integrating open, transparent, and reproducible practices into undergraduate and graduate curricula and research training.
Embedding Open Science principles early—through hands-on replication projects, transparent coding assignments, and discussions of research integrity—normalizes these practices for the next generation of scientists and improves pedagogical outcomes.

🎓 Step 7: Teaching Open Science (Sustaining the Movement)

The Educational Gap: Addressing the reality that a vast majority of students currently graduate from statistics courses having never heard of the replication crisis [INDEX].
A 1-Hour Practical Footprint: Deploying structured 1-hour introductory modules to completely pivot how incoming researchers view media claims and data transparency [INDEX].
The Dual Psychological Impact: Training students to trust unverified research less while simultaneously causing them to view their field as closer to the hard natural sciences [INDEX].
Training Future Consumers: Realizing that open science pedagogy is vital even for students who leave research, creating critical public consumers of data [INDEX].
Leveraging Existing Infrastructure: Utilizing free, collaborative open platforms like FORRT and the Open Science MOOC to drop pre-built resources straight into existing syllabi [INDEX].

Engage Fully: Be ready to speak, debate, and share ideas.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
text:
Why Are We Here?

The Shift: Computation-based research is transitioning toward Frictionless Reproducibility (FR).
The Triad: FR driven by maturity of 3 data science principles:

data sharing
code sharing
competitive challenges

The Superpower: Empirical Machine Learning (EML) uses this triad as an emergent superpower to drive AI progress.
The Export: These practices can be learned and adopted by any research field to instantly accelerate its rate of progress.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
section: The Old Way vs. The New Way
text:
The Old Way vs. The New Way
The Old Way (In-Principle Sharing)

A scientist publishes a paper with a beautiful chart.
If you want to check it, you have to email them,
Wait weeks for the data,
figure out their messy code,
and fix a dozen errors.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
section: The Old Way vs. The New Way
text:
The Old Way vs. The New Way
The New Way (Frictionless Reproducibility)

You read a paper,
click a link,
clone their GitHub repository,
and run their exact analysis on your laptop in 2 minutes.


The “Singularity”
When checking other people’s data work becomes effortless, scientific progress explodes at breakneck speed.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
text:
Cheap and Massive Compute Power

The Stalled Engine: Around 2005, individual computer chips stopped getting significantly faster year-over-year.
The Smartphone Boom: Because billions of people bought smartphones, tech companies built a massive global network of cloud servers to handle all that data.
The Result for Data Science: Today, any undergraduate student with a laptop can rent a supercomputer on the cloud for pennies to run massive datasets. Space and processing power are no longer bottlenecks.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
text:
Data Science Matures
The Core Triad:

Open Data: Exposing the raw numbers, not just summaries.
Open Code: Sharing the exact scripts so others can re-run the math.
Common Challenges: A shared goal where everyone uses the same dataset to compete for the best accuracy scores on a public leaderboard.


Phase Transition: When all three legs of the triad meet, researchers can reproduce or modify an outside institution’s results within minutes or clicks.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
section: What Happens If You Hide One Leg?
text:
What Happens If You Hide One Leg?


🛑 No Challenges

You get “Open Science” but no common goal.
Everyone works in isolated bubbles.
Impossible to rank which method actually works best.


🛑 No Code

You get competitions with secret methods (like the Netflix Prize).
People win, but no one learns how they won because the code is locked.


🛑 No Data

You get “Bring-Your-Own-Data” science (like private medical trials).
You cannot verify the claims because the underlying data is a black box.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
text:
Viral Science: Zero Friction
The Meme Analogy  Why do internet memes spread across the globe in a single afternoon? Because there is zero friction to share them—you just click “forward.”

Viral Code: When data, code, and leaderboards are completely open, scientific ideas spread through a research community exactly like viral memes.
The “URL or I Don’t Care” Rule: Modern data analysts reject paywalls and broken links. If a research method doesn’t have an immediate, working link, the community ignores it and moves on.

title: Data Science at the Singularity
text:
Automated Science Tracking

Code as Gold: In the future, public code repositories will be treated as raw material.
Automated Tweaking: Data scientists will write automated scripts designed to crawl through thousands of past papers, pull down their code, and automatically swap parameters to find hidden improvements.
The Backwater Risk: Research fields that refuse to share their data and code due to privacy or copyright fears will be left behind and forgotten by the next generation.

Project Organization
When starting a new project, it is worthwhile to spend some time thinking about how to best organize its content.

This means asking questions such as:

What are my project inputs?
What types of outputs do I expect to come out of this project?
How does this project relate to other projects I am working on?

title: Project Organization
section: When you begin a new project …
text:
When you begin a new project …

It is generally a good idea to store all of the files relevant to one project under a common root directory.
The exception to this rule is source code or scripts that are used in multiple projects. Each such program might have a project directory of its own.

title: Project Organization
text:
Golden rules

Raw data should never be changed. Save it into a data/ folder and treat it as immutable.
The processed, clean version of your data will go into a dedicated file or directory, e.g., clean_data.json or processed_data/.
Anything that can be generated from code goes into its own folder.

output/, results/, images/

If there are text documents, put them in their own folder:

docs/

title: Project Organization
text:
Golden rules (cont’d)

Code also has its own folder: code/.

If you write a lot of functions, then create a functions/ folder
Or also a src/ (for source) folder to save processing/analysis code.

If processing/analysis scripts are meant to be used in a certain order, you can number them:

e.g., script1-data-prepration.R, script2-exploratory-analysis.R, script3-regression-model.R, etc.

Sometimes the pipeline is not linear but branched, so numbering may not always make sense.
Modularize your code: split a giant script into short, single-purpose scripts with well-defined inputs and outputs.

title: Project Organization
text:
Golden rules (cont’d)

A project directory should be a portable island.
It can be zipped up, moved to a different folder, sent to a colleague, or cloned onto a remote server …
… and every script still runs without modifying a single line of code.

title: Project Organization
text:
Documentation (README files)

Each of your projects should always be accompanied by a README file.
The README should contain all the information an outsider would need to understand what the project is all about:

what are the inputs
what are the outputs,
where to find files within the project directory, etc.

The README is simply a text file, there’s nothing special to it.

I like to write it in markdown syntax: README.md

Writing down everything about a project in a README.md can be tedious, but it pays off.

title: Project Organization
text:
README file(s)

Record who the author/s is/are,
the date the project was started,
a description of what the project is for,
describe important details
(a README file is sort of a growing/living document)


Get in the habit of starting a project by creating a README file.
Also, you can include README files inside the project’s directories: e.g. a README for the data/ folder, or for the docs/ filder.

title: Project Organization
text:
Some Comments

How you define a project is largely up to you.
It could be all the work you do on a given dataset,
Or all the work you do for a thesis or dissertation,
Or each manuscript could be its own project even if it uses the same dataset as a different project.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Limitations of local repos

It only exists on one computer

If your hard drive fails, you could lose all your work and history unless you have backups.

Make collaboration difficult

If you’re working with teammates, there’s no easy way for them to see your changes or contribute to your project.
Sharing code from a local repository requires manual file transfers or email attachments.

Solution?

Remote repositories!

title: Git Remotes
section: Basic Workflow with a Remote Repository
text:
Basic Workflow with a Remote Repository



You synchronize your local repo with a remote repo.
You do your day-to-day work in a local repository.
You upload your local changes to the remote repo.
Repeat steps 2-3

title: Git Remotes
text:
In most real-world Git workflows, you use both local and remote repositories together. You do your day-to-day work in a local repository, and you synchronize with a remote repository to share changes and collaborate.
This dual-repository model gives you the best of both worlds: the speed and privacy of local work combined with the backup and collaboration benefits of remote hosting.

title: Git Remotes
text:
What is a remote repository?



A remote repository is a copy of your Git project hosted on a server that is accessible over the internet or a network.

Your local repo sits on your computer
The remote repo lives on a centralized infrastructure


Simply put, a remote repo is just another git repository that is stored (hosted) in a remote computer (as opposed to local repos stored in your computer).

title: Git Remotes
section: What is a remote repo good for?
text:
What is a remote repo good for?



Two primary purposes:

Remote repositories are good for collaboration1
They are also good as a backup (or “solitary reproducibility”)


We’ll discuss how to use remote repos for collaboration in a future lecture.

title: Git Remotes
section: Why Remotes Matter for Solitary Reproducibility?
text:
Why Remotes Matter for Solitary Reproducibility?

Offsite Backup & Disaster recovery: Protects research from local hardware failures.
Hardware Mobility: Seamlessly move code between a laptop and a lab’s computing cluster.
Public Provenance: Serves as a timestamped, immutable record of scientific development.
Public Inspection: True reproducibility requires third-party verification. Remote repos allow peer-reviewers and the public to audit your work.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Platforms to host remote repositories

GitHub: The industry standard and largest host in the world. It is the default platform for open-source software, academic packages, and community-driven reproducible research.
GitLab: A powerful alternative heavily favored by enterprises and institutional research centers. Many universities host their own self-managed GitLab instances on internal servers to comply with strict data privacy laws.
Bitbucket: Owned by Atlassian, this platform is frequently used in corporate environments that rely heavily on Jira for project management.


BTW: We’re going to focus on GitHub. You’ll get formally introduced to GitHub in lab.

title: Git Remotes
text:
About GitHub

Web-based platform that hosts Git repositories in the cloud.
Used by developers store, share, and collaborate on software code.
Created in 2008; Acquired by Microsoft in 2018.
Provides:

a user-friendly graphical interface,
project management features,
automation tools on top of the standard command-line Git environment

GitHub \(\neq\) Git

Git is the local version control engine,
GitHub is the global distribution hub.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Limitations of Remote Repositories

Working with remote repositories requires internet connectivity.
Remote repositories introduce an extra step in your workflow. After making local commits, you need to explicitly upload them to the remote repo.
Hosting service issues:

storage limits,
privacy concerns,
costs ($)



Depending on the hosting service, there may be storage limits, privacy concerns, or costs associated with private repositories, though many platforms offer free tiers for personal and open-source projects.

title: Git Remotes
text:
What happens during git push?
When you run git push origin main

Git checks which commits exist locally but not on the remote.
Git compresses these commits and sends them to GitHub.
GitHub receives the commits and updates the remote branch.
GitHub sends a confirmation message back to your local Git.
The moment the local Git engine receives that success confirmation from GitHub, it instantly updates the local origin/main pointer forward to the last commit.
Local main and local origin/main are perfectly aligned, pointing to the last commit.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Demistifying origin

Analogy:

📇 Contact Name: origin
📲 Phone Number: git@github.com:yourusername/your-repo.git

origin is just a shortcut nickname.
It is NOT the name of a branch
Why use it? Typing long cryptographic SSH URLs every time you save your work is annoying.
The Mapping: Git maps the short nickname origin to your specific, secure URL on GitHub.
Flexibility: You could technically rename origin to github, backup, or cloud (Git doesn’t care!)

title: Git Remotes
text:
Demistifying origin/main

this is the remote-tracking branch
it is a local branch (lives on your computer, not in the cloud)
it is read-only (git manages it automatically)
the format is always server/branch
i.e. the main branch that lives on the origin server
it acts as a cache or a local bookmark
it only moves when your computer speaks to github (via push, fetch, pull)
origin/main is like a contact’s “Last Seen” timestamp. It doesn’t track what GitHub is doing in real-time;
it only tracks what GitHub was doing the last time you interacted with it


Its sole job is to answer the question: “Where was the GitHub server’s main branch the absolute last time this laptop talked to it?

title: Git Remotes
text:
Local -vs- Remote


Local Repo

Located on your hard drive
Only you can access it directly
Works completly offline
Very fast (local disk operations)
No automatic backup
Difficult to share with others
Completely private


Remote Repo

Located on a server or cloud
Multiple users can access it
Internet required
Slower (network-dependent)
Acts as a backup for local work
Designed for team collaboration
Can be public or private

title: Git Remotes
text:
Basic git push syntax
The simplest form of git push looks like this:

git push <remote> <branch>

<remote> is the name of your remote repository (usually origin)
<branch> is the branch you want to push



For example, to push your main branch to the remote called origin:
git push origin main

title: Git Remotes
section: Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
text:
Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
Assume that the URL of the remote repository is: git@github.com:yourusername/your-repo.git



Step 1) Adding a remote is straightforward:
git remote add origin [repository-url]

git remote add: The command to add a new remote connection
origin: The name you’re giving to this remote (convention is to use "origin")
[repository-url]: The GitHub URL you copied earlier

title: Git Remotes
section: Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
text:
Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
Step 2) Once a remote repo has been added, check your remote connection

git remote -v




You should see output like this:
origin  git@github.com:yourusername/your-repo.git (fetch)
origin  git@github.com:yourusername/your-repo.git (push)
This confirms that origin points to your GitHub repository.

title: Git Remotes
section: Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
text:
Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
Step 3) Make sure you have commits
# View your commits
git log --oneline


If you see commits listed, you’re ready to push. If not, make some changes and commit them first.

title: Git Remotes
section: Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
text:
Pushing Your First Commit to GitHub
Step 4) Now push your commits to GitHub:
# Push main branch to origin
git push origin main



For your first push, you might see output like this:
Enumerating objects: 3, done.
Counting objects: 100% (3/3), done.
Writing objects: 100% (3/3), 242 bytes | 242.00 KiB/s, done.
Total 3 (delta 0), reused 0 (delta 0)
To git@github.com:yourusername/your-repo.git
 * [new branch]      main -> main

title: Git Remotes
text:
Setting Upstream Tracking

Every time you push, you might get tired of typing git push origin main.
Git offers a shortcut using upstream tracking.


# Push and set upstream tracking
git push -u origin main

When you set an upstream branch, Git remembers which remote branch corresponds to your local branch.
Then you can just type git push without specifying the remote and branch.
Now you can simply use:



# Short form (works after setting upstream)
git push

title: Git Remotes
text:
Pushing Multiple Commits at Once

You don’t need to push after every commit.
Git lets you accumulate multiple commits locally and push them all at once.


Example:

Say you have 3 new commits in your local branch.
You can push all three commits at once:



git push origin main


Git will send all three commits to GitHub in a single push operation. This is more efficient than pushing after each individual commit.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Pushing Different Branches

You can push any local branch to GitHub, not just main.
This is useful when working on features or bug fixes.


Example: Say you created a feature branch called add-login (and made some commits):


To push this branch to GitHub:
git push -u origin add-login

title: Git Remotes
text:
When to push your code
There’s no strict rule, but here are some good practices:

After completing a logical unit of work: When you finish a feature, fix a bug, or reach a stable state.
Before ending your work session: Push at the end of the day so your work is backed up.
Before switching computers: Push from one machine so you can pull on another.
When collaborating: Push regularly so teammates can see your progress.


Avoid pushing broken code or work-in-progress changes to the main branch. Use feature branches for incomplete work.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Error: Updates Were Rejected
This error happens when the remote branch has commits that you don’t have locally:
! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 
'git@github.com:yourusername/your-repo.git'

hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains 
work that you do not have locally.



This typically means someone else pushed changes to GitHub, or you made commits on GitHub directly (like editing files in the web interface).
Solution: You need to pull the remote changes first, then push again. We’ll cover git pull in a future lecture.
git pull origin main

title: Git Remotes
text:
Error: No Upstream Branch
If you try to use git push without setting upstream tracking first, you’ll see:
fatal: The current branch main has no upstream branch.



Solution: Set the upstream when you push:
git push -u origin main

title: Git Remotes
text:
Error: Authentication Failed
If your credentials are incorrect or expired, you’ll see:
remote: Invalid username or password.
fatal: Authentication failed

 
Solution: Check GitHub’s authentication settings.

title: Git Remotes
text:
Best Practices for Pushing
Follow these guidelines to avoid common problems:

Always commit before pushing: You can’t push uncommitted changes.
Use meaningful commit messages: Others will see your commits on GitHub.
Pull before pushing: Especially in team projects, check for remote changes first.
Push feature branches separately: Keep experimental work isolated from main.
Don’t force push: Avoid git push --force unless you understand the consequences.

Many teams follow a strict prefix naming system to categorize changes. This makes the Git log easily machine-readable for automated changelogs.

Keeps Repositories Clean: It prevents junk files like system logs (.log), temporary folders, and OS-generated files (like Mac’s .DS_Store) from cluttering your repository.
Secures Private Data: It blocks you from accidentally uploading sensitive credentials, API keys, passwords, or configuration files (like .env) to public platforms like GitHub.
Saves Storage Space: It keeps massive data directories, external libraries (like Node’s node_modules or Python’s venv), and heavy compiled binaries out of your Git history.

title: Intro to Git (part 2)
text:
The “Golden Rule” of .gitignore


Warning: Git can only ignore untracked files!


If you commit a file first, and then add it to your .gitignore later, Git will continue to track it.


To fix this and force Git to honor the new rule, you have to manually remove the file from your active staging cache using the command:  git rm --cached <filename>
